CH2 · UNIT 02 · MODULE 2.4

Decomposition & Nutrient Cycles

Energy passes through an ecosystem once, but atoms are used again and again. Part 1 is how dead matter gets turned back into nutrients. Part 2 meets the decomposers, above all the fungi. Part 3 follows nitrogen and phosphorus around the loop, and shows what happens when we overload it.

MODULE 2.4 · PART 1

Matter cycles, and decomposition closes the loop

THE QUESTION Every living thing eventually dies. What turns a dead leaf back into something a plant can use, and what decides how fast that happens?

Seven steps: why matter cycles, what really moves when something is eaten, the law that makes it possible, what decomposition does, what sets its speed, why some dead matter lasts longer, and the animals that shred it.

STEP 1 · START HERE

Energy flows. Matter cycles.

Module 2.3 ended with energy leaving every food web as heat. Matter is different. The atoms an organism is made of are never used up. They are passed on, taken apart, and built into something new.

DIAGRAM · A LINE AND A LOOP

Two different journeys

ENERGY
passes through onceMATTER · goes aroundProducersConsumersheatsunProducersConsumersDetritusNutrients

"Matter" means atoms: carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and the other elements living things are built from. They cycle between organisms and the abiotic environment: the soil, the water and the air.

THREE WORDS FOR NUTRIENTS

Essential, macro, limiting

ESSENTIAL NUTRIENTAn element required for growth, reproduction or metabolic function.
MACRONUTRIENTNeeded in large quantities. Macronutrients are the building blocks of proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates and phospholipids.
LIMITING NUTRIENTOne that limits the growth of primary producers when it is in short supply, which it often is. Nitrogen and phosphorus are limiting in some ecosystems.
COMMON MIX-UP · MACRO DOES NOT MEAN A BIG MOLECULE "Macro" is about how much an organism needs, not about the size of anything. Nitrogen is a macronutrient because living things need a lot of it. The word for a large molecule is macromolecule. The two are linked, which is why they get mixed up: macronutrients are what macromolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids are built from.
INTERACTIVE · ONE CYCLE, THREE PARTS

A biogeochemical cycle

Tap a button to explore
AIRN₂ gasNH₄⁺ · NO₃⁻SOILWATERa planta giraffeeatenbacteria +
archaea
change ittaken updeath and waste,
then decomposition
BIOPart of the journey is inside living thingsNitrogen atoms sit inside organisms as part of their proteins and nucleic acids. They move along the food chain when one organism eats another.Example: a nitrogen atom in a leaf protein, then in a giraffe protein.
GEOPart of it is in the non-living worldBetween organisms, the atom sits in a pool that is not alive: the atmosphere, the soil, or water.Example: most of Earth's nitrogen is in the air as N₂ gas. In soil and water it is found as ammonium and nitrate.
CHEMICALThe same atom, in a different molecule at every stopThe element is never changed into another element. What changes is the molecule it is part of.Example: N₂ gas in the air → ammonium (NH₄⁺) and nitrate (NO₃⁻), made by bacteria and archaea → proteins and nucleic acids, built by a plant (assimilation) → back to an inorganic form when the organism dies and is decomposed.
TAP EACH PART OF THE WORDbio + geo + chemicalThe drawing shows one cycle, nitrogen, with all three parts in it at once. Tap a button to light up one part and see an example.
THE NAME FOR THE LOOP

What the word means

A biogeochemical cycle is the path an element takes as it moves from one pool to another within an ecosystem.

BIOSome of the pools are living things.
GEOSome are the non-living Earth: air, soil, water, rock.
CHEMICALThe element is built into different molecules as it moves.

This module follows two elements: nitrogen and phosphorus. Carbon is Module 2.5.

Check yourself: when nitrogen moves from the soil into a plant, is that the bio part, the geo part, or the chemical part?

All three at once. The atom leaves a geo pool (soil), enters a bio pool (the plant), and changes molecule on the way (from ammonium or nitrate into a protein). That is why it is one word.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Essential nutrient

An element that is required for growth, reproduction or metabolic function.

Macronutrient

A nutrient needed in large quantities. Macronutrients are the building blocks of proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates and phospholipids.

Limiting nutrient

A nutrient that limits the growth of primary producers when it is in short supply. Nitrogen and phosphorus are limiting in some ecosystems.

Biogeochemical cycle

The path an element takes as it moves from one pool to another within an ecosystem.

STEP 2 · WHAT ACTUALLY MOVES

A giraffe eats a leaf. Where does the protein go?

The leaf contains protein. Does that same protein molecule end up in the giraffe? No. The molecule is taken apart. Its atoms are what move.

DIAGRAM · ONE PROTEIN, FOLLOWED THROUGH A MEAL

Same beads, different chain

PROTEIN
IN THE LEAFAMINO
ACIDSPROTEIN IN
THE GIRAFFEdigestion
chain taken apartbiosynthesis
a new chain built

Each bead is an amino acid, and each one carries nitrogen (N). The giraffe ends up with the leaf's nitrogen atoms, built into giraffe proteins. It is not the same protein that was in the leaf.

THE THREE THINGS THAT HAPPEN

Eat, take apart, rebuild

1Eaten
The leaf's protein enters the giraffe's gut as a large organic molecule.
2Digested
Enzymes break it into its building blocks, amino acids, which are small enough to absorb.
3Rebuilt
The giraffe's cells join those amino acids into its own proteins. Building new organic molecules is biosynthesis.
THE RULE FOR THIS WHOLE MODULE Molecules are built, broken and rebuilt. Atoms are passed on. When you trace a nutrient, trace the atom and name the molecule it is in at each stop.
INTERACTIVE · WHERE THE NITROGEN SITS

Protein, DNA and RNA all contain nitrogen

Tap a button to explore
PROTEINDNARNAN in every
amino acidN in every
baseN in every
base
PROTEINNitrogen in every amino acidA protein is a chain of amino acids, and every amino acid contains nitrogen. So every protein does: muscle, enzymes, the proteins in a leaf.
DNANitrogen in every baseThe rungs of the ladder are the bases (A, T, G and C), and every base contains nitrogen. DNA also contains phosphorus, in the two long strands that hold the rungs.
RNAThe same againRNA is a single strand with bases (A, U, G and C) hanging from it. Every base contains nitrogen. DNA and RNA together are the nucleic acids.
TAP A MOLECULEThree places a nitrogen atom ends upEvery pink N is a nitrogen atom. When you hear "organisms need nitrogen", these are the molecules it is needed for.
WHY IT IS NOT ONLY ABOUT PROTEIN

The giraffe needs nitrogen for all three

The amino acids from the leaf are not only rebuilt into protein. Their nitrogen atoms are also used to build the giraffe's DNA and RNA.

NITROGEN IS INProteins and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA).
PHOSPHORUS IS INNucleic acids, ATP and phospholipids. Part 3 comes back to this.
Check yourself: a lion eats the giraffe. Is the leaf's nitrogen atom now in the lion?

It can be. The giraffe's protein is digested into amino acids, and the lion builds them into lion proteins or uses the nitrogen for its own DNA and RNA. Same atom, third molecule.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Organic

Carbon-containing molecules such as carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids. CO₂ is inorganic carbon.

Inorganic

Not organic. Ammonium, nitrate, phosphate, CO₂ and N₂ gas are inorganic.

Biosynthesis

Building new organic molecules, such as proteins and nucleic acids.

STEP 3 · THE LAW BEHIND IT

Atoms are never used up: conservation of mass

Why can matter cycle at all? Because of one law. Matter is not created or destroyed. In living things and in ecosystems, atoms are only rearranged into new molecules and passed on.

INTERACTIVE · FOLLOW ONE ATOM THROUGH TIME

Could an atom from a dinosaur be in you?

Tap the buttons, or Next stop, to click through all 5
ONE NITROGEN ATOM · MILLIONS OF YEARS →dinosaursoilplantanimalyouthe atom is in a protein in the dinosaurthe atom is in ammonium (NH₄⁺) in the soilthe atom is in a protein in a leafthe atom is in a protein in the animalthe atom is in a protein, or the DNA, of one of your cells
STOP 1 · LONG AGOA nitrogen atom is part of a dinosaurIt sits in a protein in the dinosaur's body. The dinosaur got it the way the giraffe did: from its food.
STOP 2 · THE DINOSAUR DIESDecomposers take the protein apartThe protein is broken down. The nitrogen atom is released into the soil as part of an inorganic molecule, ammonium. The atom is not destroyed. Only the molecule is.
STOP 3 · A PLANT TAKES IT UPBack into a living thingA plant's roots take up the ammonium, and the plant builds the nitrogen atom into one of its own proteins.
STOP 4 · AND AGAIN, AND AGAINAround the loop, over and overAn animal eats the plant. It dies, is decomposed, and the atom is taken up by another plant. This loop can repeat for millions of years, because nothing in it uses the atom up.
STOP 5 · TODAYThe same atom, in youYou eat. The atom is built into one of your proteins, or into your DNA. An atom that was once part of a dinosaur really can be part of you, because of the law of conservation of mass.This particular route is made up to show the idea. Nobody can follow a single atom. The principle is what is real.
THE LAW OF CONSERVATION OF MASS

What it says, and what follows from it

THE LAWAtoms are not created and not destroyed by eating, digestion, growth, death or decomposition.
SOEvery atom in a living thing came from somewhere, and when the organism dies every one of them goes somewhere.
WHICH MEANSThe atoms on Earth are reused. That is what "matter cycles" means.
MATTER AND ENERGY ARE BOTH CONSERVED

So why does only matter cycle?

MATTERStays on Earth as the same atoms, so it can be used again and again: a loop.
ENERGYIs conserved too, but it ends up as heat, which organisms cannot reuse and which leaves for space. So it has to keep arriving from the sun: a one-way flow.
Check yourself: a fallen log slowly rots away until nothing is left. Were its atoms destroyed?

No. Decomposers turned its organic molecules into carbon dioxide and water, which went into the air, and into nutrients that went into the soil. Every atom still exists. It is just somewhere else, in a different molecule.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Conservation of mass

Matter is not created or destroyed. In an ecosystem, atoms are rearranged into new molecules and passed on, never used up.

STEP 4 · WHAT CLOSES THE LOOP

Decomposition: organic molecules in, inorganic nutrients out

Producers can only take up nutrients in simple inorganic forms. Everything that dies is made of complex organic molecules. Decomposition is the conversion of one back into the other. Hold on to this one sentence before meeting any decomposer by name.

DIAGRAM · THE ONE THING DECOMPOSITION DOES

Big organic molecules become small inorganic ones

ORGANIC
in detritusINORGANIC
in soil and waterDECOMPOSERSproteins, DNA, RNA
big and complexNH₄⁺NO₃⁻PO₄³⁻small and simple:
producers can
take these up

Decomposition starts with organic molecules and ends with inorganic ones. Those inorganic forms are exactly the ones producers can use.

THE THREE FORMS TO KNOW BY NAME

Ammonium, nitrate, phosphate

AMMONIUM · NH₄⁺Inorganic nitrogen. This is the form nitrogen is in when decomposition releases it from proteins and nucleic acids.
NITRATE · NO₃⁻Inorganic nitrogen too. Other microbes in the soil make it from ammonium. Part 3 shows that step.
PHOSPHATE · PO₄³⁻Inorganic phosphorus, released from nucleic acids, ATP and phospholipids.

Producers take up all three and build them back into organic molecules. The loop is closed.

ENERGY DOES NOT COME BACK Decomposers recycle the atoms in detritus. They do not recycle its energy. They use that energy to live, and it leaves as heat, just as it does at every other level of a food web.
DIAGRAM · FROM A DEAD LEAF BACK TO A LIVING ONE

The same thing, out in the soil

DETRITUS
dead matter
and wasteDETRITIVORE
shreds itDECOMPOSERS · bacteria, archaea, fungiNH₄⁺ PO₄³⁻PRODUCER
takes them upORGANIC →→ INORGANIC

Decomposers move nutrients from the detrital pool back to the abiotic environment, where producers can use them. The next three steps look at how fast this goes and who does it.

WHY IT MATTERS

Without decomposers, everything stops

Nutrients would stay locked inside dead bodies and waste. Producers would run out of nitrogen and phosphorus to take up, primary production would stop, and so would every food web built on it.

That is why decomposition is behind ecosystem services such as primary production. And it sets the pace: the rate of decomposition limits how fast nutrients move through an ecosystem.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Detritus

Dead matter and waste. Detritus is a pool, not a flux.

Decomposers

Bacteria, archaea, fungi and a few other eukaryotes that break complex organic molecules down into inorganic forms.

Decomposition

The breakdown of detritus into inorganic forms that producers can use again.

Ecosystem services

Benefits that ecosystems provide, such as primary production. They depend on nutrients being recycled.

STEP 5 · HOW FAST?

What controls the rate: temperature, water and oxygen

Decomposers are living things, so anything that speeds up or slows down their metabolism changes how fast nutrients are recycled.

INTERACTIVE · DATA · DECOMPOSER ACTIVITY IN SOIL

Temperature and water both matter

Tap the labels on the picture
0.51.01.520406080100SOIL WATER CONTENT (%) →DECOMPOSER ACTIVITY ↑too dryabout righttoo wet
COLD SOIL · 10 °CSlow, whatever the moistureThe line stays near the bottom of the graph. Enzymes work slowly in the cold, so decomposers get little done even when water is just right.
WARM SOIL · 20 °CFaster, with a clear best moistureActivity climbs as dry soil gets wetter, peaks at moderate water content, and drops when the soil is soaked.
HOT SOIL · 30 °CFastest of the threeAt the same water content, this line is far above the other two. Warmth speeds decomposers up. It still falls at both ends: too dry, and too wet.
TAP A TEMPERATURE ON THE GRAPHEach line is one soil temperatureCompare the three lines to see the effect of temperature. Follow one line from left to right to see the effect of water.

Decomposer activity is measured here as soil microbial respiration (mg of carbon per day).

ON LAND · READ THEM OFF THE GRAPH

Two controls you can see

TEMPERATUREWarmer is faster, across the range measured here. The 30 °C line sits above 20 °C, which sits above 10 °C. It is not a rule without limits: decomposers are living things, and every organism has a temperature that is too hot for it.
MOISTUREModerate is fastest. Too dry, and decomposers cannot work. Too wet, and they run out of oxygen.
Check yourself: does the graph show the effect of temperature, of soil water content, or of both?

Both. The three separate lines show temperature. The rise and fall along each line shows water content.

INTERACTIVE · THE HIDDEN THIRD CONTROL

Oxygen: why soaked soil decomposes slowly

Tap a button to explore
DAMP SOILWATERLOGGED SOILthin leaf layerdead plants pile upair gaps · O₂all water · no O₂
DAMP, WITH AIR IN ITWater and oxygen at the same timeThe gaps between soil grains hold some water and some air. Decomposers have both things they need, so dead matter is broken down about as fast as it falls.This is the middle of every line on the graph above: the peak.
WATERLOGGEDPlenty of water, no oxygenWater has filled every gap and pushed the air out. Oxygen runs short, so decay goes slowly, or hardly at all. Dead plant matter piles up faster than it is broken down.This is the right-hand end of every line on the graph: the drop in very wet soil. Over a very long time, buried piles of undecayed plants like this are what become coal, which is where Module 2.5 picks up.
TAP A SOILWhy does too much water slow decomposition?The blue dots are oxygen. The purple shapes are decomposers. Compare what is in the gaps, and what has built up on top.
WHY OXYGEN MATTERS SO MUCH

Decomposers respire, like you do

Most decomposers get energy from organic molecules by cellular respiration, the same reaction your own cells run. It needs oxygen.

INGREDIENTSorganic molecule+O₂
PRODUCTSCO₂+water+heat

Take the oxygen away and the reaction stalls. Fungi in particular need oxygen to break down wood.

WHERE OXYGEN RUNS SHORTWaterlogged soils, bogs and swamps. Dead plants build up there instead of rotting.
THE SAME IDEA, LATER IN THIS MODULEIn a dead zone it runs the other way: a burst of decomposition uses up the oxygen in the water.
THE REST OF THE LIST

Two more things set the rate

QUALITY OF THE DETRITUSWhat the dead matter is made of. That is the next step.
IN WATERTemperature is a key driver of decomposition rates in aquatic environments. Part 2 ends on the deep-sea floor, where it is very cold.
STEP 6 · WHAT IS IT MADE OF?

The quality of the detritus

Temperature, water and oxygen are about the conditions. The last control is about the dead matter itself. Not all detritus is equally easy to decompose.

INTERACTIVE · THREE KINDS OF DEAD MATTER

Why a leaf rots faster than a log

Tap a button to explore
SOFT TISSUE
loose moleculesCELLULOSE
tightly packedWOOD
plus ligninbreaks down
FASTbreaks down
more slowlybreaks down
SLOWESTpink shapes = decomposers' enzymes
HIGH QUALITYEasy to get into, and rewardingSoft tissue that is rich in nutrients, such as a fresh green leaf, fruit, or animal remains. Enzymes can reach the molecules easily, so it disappears quickly.
LOWER QUALITYCellulose: a complex carbohydrateCellulose is the main material of plant cell walls. It is a long chain of glucose, so it is rich in carbon and energy. But the chains bind tightly to one another, which makes it hard to break down. Tough leaves and stems take longer.
LOWEST QUALITYWood: cellulose locked inside ligninIn wood, the cellulose is wrapped in lignin, a tough material with no regular structure for an enzyme to grip. A few bacteria can break lignin down, but in nature fungi do most of the decomposition of wood, and they need oxygen to do it.That is why a log can lie on a forest floor for years after the leaves around it are long gone.
TAP A KIND OF DETRITUSZoom in to the molecules"Quality" is how easy the detritus is for decomposers to break down. Tap each box to see why one kind goes faster than another.
WHAT "QUALITY" MEANS HERE

Quality is from the decomposer's point of view

The quality of detritus is its chemistry: what it is made of, and so how easy it is for decomposers to break down and how much they get out of it.

HIGH-QUALITY DETRITUSRich in nitrogen, low in lignin. Soft tissue such as green leaves. Decomposes quickly, so its nutrients are back in circulation soon.
LOW-QUALITY DETRITUSPoor in nitrogen, high in lignin and other tough structural material. Wood, bark, needles. Decomposes slowly, so its nutrients stay locked up for longer.
THINK OF YOUR OWN FOOD Sugar is digested quickly. A bowl of whole grains, which is complex carbohydrate and fiber, takes much longer and keeps you going for longer. Detritus works the same way: the more complex and tough the molecules, the longer it lasts.
WATCH THE WORD In everyday talk the slow, complex food is the "healthy" one. In ecology the word runs the other way: high quality means it breaks down fast, and low quality means it breaks down slowly.
Check yourself: two forests are equally warm and wet. One drops soft leaves, the other drops tough needles and a lot of wood. In which do nutrients cycle faster?

The one with soft leaves. Its detritus is higher quality, so decomposition is faster, and the rate of decomposition is what limits how fast nutrients move through an ecosystem.

STEP 7 · THE SHREDDERS

Detritivores: animals that break detritus into pieces

Before the chemistry there is often a mechanical step. Animals eat the detritus and break it into much smaller pieces. That does not finish the job, but it makes the job far faster.

INTERACTIVE · WHY SMALLER PIECES ROT FASTER

Surface area for the same volume

Tap the buttons, or Shred it, to click through all 2
1 piece · decomposers reach only the outside9 pieces · 3 times as much surfacepurple dots =
decomposers
BEFORE · ONE BIG PIECEOnly the outside can be worked onDecomposers work on surfaces. With one big piece, everything in the middle is out of reach until the outside is gone.
AFTER · A DETRITIVORE HAS BEEN AT ITSame leaf, far more surfaceThe amount of leaf has not changed. But cutting it in three each way gives three times as much surface for the same volume: a higher surface-to-volume ratio. Decomposers can now work on all of it at once, so it breaks down much faster.It is the reason you chew your food before your stomach digests it.
SCENE · WHO THEY ARE

Earthworms, termites, dung beetles

DETRITIVORES · animals that eat detritusEARTHWORMTERMITEDUNG BEETLEdead leaves, soildead wooddung

Others include millipedes on land, and many crabs and lobsters on the sea floor.

TWO JOBS, TWO NAMES

Detritivore vs. decomposer

DETRITIVORESAnimals that eat detritus. They break it into smaller pieces physically, which gives decomposers more surface to work on.
DECOMPOSERSBacteria, archaea, fungi, and a few other eukaryotes. They break complex organic molecules down chemically into inorganic forms.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Detritivore

An animal that eats detritus and breaks it into smaller pieces, such as an earthworm, a termite or a dung beetle.

Lock it in · Part 1

  1. Energy flows through once. Matter cycles: the same atoms move between organisms and the abiotic environment.
  2. A macronutrient is one needed in large quantities. It is not a large molecule.
  3. When something is eaten, its molecules are taken apart and rebuilt. The atoms are what get passed on. Nitrogen ends up in proteins, DNA and RNA.
  4. Conservation of mass: atoms are never created or destroyed, only rearranged. That is why matter can cycle.
  5. Decomposition turns organic molecules in detritus into inorganic forms producers can use: ammonium, nitrate and phosphate.
  6. Decomposition is faster when it is warm, when moisture is moderate, when there is oxygen, and when the detritus is high quality (soft, not woody).
  7. Detritivores are animals that eat and shred detritus. Smaller pieces have more surface for their volume, so decomposers work faster.
MODULE 2.4 · PART 2

The decomposers: fungi and whale falls

THE QUESTION Something has to do the work of decomposition. What kind of living thing is it, and why is most of it hidden?

Eight steps: one word that describes them all, the biology of fungi, how a fungus eats, why its wall is chitin, the forest beneath the forest, where fungi are most diverse, fungi that feed plants, and what happens to a whale on the sea floor.

STEP 1 · A WORD FIRST, THEN THE CAST

Who the decomposers are

Part 1 was about what decomposition does. This part is about who does it. One word describes how nearly all of them live, so learn it before you meet them.

INTERACTIVE · TAKE THE WORD APART

Chemo · hetero · troph

Tap a button to explore
energy from
chemicalscarbon from
other organismsfeedingfoodan organic molecule,
such as glucoseENERGYCARBON
to build with
CHEMO · WHERE THE ENERGY COMES FROMFrom chemicals, not from lightA chemotroph gets its energy by breaking chemical bonds in molecules. The opposite is photo: energy from sunlight.
HETERO · WHERE THE CARBON COMES FROMFrom other organismsHetero means "other". A heterotroph gets its carbon from organic molecules that some other organism made. The opposite is auto, "self": carbon taken straight from CO₂.
TROPH · FEEDINGIt is a word about how something feeds itselfPut together: a chemoheterotroph gets both its energy and its carbon from organic molecules. One molecule of glucose can supply both. You are one. So is every animal, every fungus, and many bacteria and archaea.
TAP EACH PART OF THE WORDchemo + hetero + trophOne long word, three short ideas. Learn the parts and the word never needs memorizing.
CHEMOHETEROTROPH
ENERGY FROMOrganic molecules
CARBON FROMOrganic molecules
EXAMPLEAnimals, fungi, many bacteria and archaea. Decomposers are chemoheterotrophs whose food is detritus.
PHOTOAUTOTROPH · FOR COMPARISON
ENERGY FROMSunlight
CARBON FROMCO₂
EXAMPLEPlants, algae, cyanobacteria. These are the producers that decomposers hand the nutrients back to.
DIAGRAM · WHERE THEY SIT ON THE TREE OF LIFE

Decomposers are in all three domains

BACTERIAARCHAEAplantsFUNGIanimalsEUKARYAclosest
relatives= has decomposersroot

The major groups are bacteria, archaea and fungi, plus a few other eukaryotes. Two of the three domains are single-celled prokaryotes. Fungi are the eukaryotes on the list.

THE CAST

Three groups to name

BACTERIAMany decomposers
ARCHAEAMany decomposers
EUKARYAFungi, and a few others

All of them do the same job: they move nutrients from the detrital pool back to the abiotic environment, by breaking complex organic molecules into inorganic forms.

A SURPRISE ON THE TREE Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants. Fungi and animals sit on the same branch of the eukaryote tree. It fits how they live: both get their carbon and energy the same way, from organic molecules.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Chemoheterotroph

An organism that gets both its energy and its carbon from organic molecules. Animals, fungi and many bacteria and archaea are chemoheterotrophs.

Decomposers

Bacteria, archaea, fungi and a few other eukaryotes that break complex organic molecules down into inorganic forms.

STEP 2 · MEET ONE GROUP PROPERLY

Fungi: the basics

Fungi are one of the major groups of decomposers, and on land they do most of the work. Four things to know about any fungus.

INTERACTIVE · HOW A FUNGUS EATS

Digestion happens outside the body

Tap a button to explore
ANIMALeat, then digestFUNGUSdigest, then absorbenzymes work
inside the gutenzymes go out,
small molecules come ina hyphadead wood
AN ANIMALFood goes inside, then gets digestedAn animal takes food into a gut. Digestive enzymes break it down inside the body, and the small molecules are absorbed from there.
A FUNGUSFood is digested outside, then taken inA fungus has no mouth and no gut. It releases digestive enzymes into whatever it is growing through, the enzymes break large molecules into small ones, and the fungus absorbs those. Digestion happens outside the body.Fungi cannot move to find food, so they grow towards it instead.
TAP ONESame kind of feeder, opposite orderBoth are chemoheterotrophs. The pink dots are digestive enzymes. Watch where they are: inside the body, or outside it.
FOUR FACTS TO KNOW

The biology of fungi

1 · DOMAINEukarya. Not plants. Their closest relatives are animals.
2 · HOW THEY EATAll fungi are chemoheterotrophs. They release digestive enzymes and then absorb nutrients, from the environment or from other organisms.
3 · CELL WALLSMade of chitin, the same material as the exoskeleton of arthropods.
4 · ONE CELL OR MANYMost are multicellular, built from threads called hyphae. A few, the yeasts, are single cells.
DIAGRAM · FACT 3

Chitin: the same stuff as a beetle's shell

CHITINfungus cell wallarthropod shellsame
material

Chitin is a tough polysaccharide that contains nitrogen. It makes a cell wall that is strong but flexible, which lets a growing thread push its way through soil and wood. Step 4 shows how.

DIAGRAM · FACT 4

Unicellular or multicellular? Both exist

YEASTS
single cellsMOST FUNGI
many cellsbread and beerthreads: hyphae
MULTICELLULAR · MOST FUNGIA body made of branching threads. This is the form that grows through soil and wood and does most of the decomposing.
UNICELLULAR · YEASTSFungi that grow as single cells and make no threads. They live where food is moist and plentiful, such as on sugary fruit. We use them to make bread and beer.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Fungi

Eukaryotes that are chemoheterotrophs. They digest food outside their bodies and absorb it, and their cell walls are made of chitin.

Chitin

The tough material in fungal cell walls. It is the same material as in the exoskeleton of arthropods.

Yeast

A fungus that grows as single cells and does not form hyphae. Yeasts are used to make bread and beer.

STEP 3 · HOW A FUNGUS EATS

Digest outside, then absorb

A fungus has no mouth and no gut. It feeds by absorbing molecules straight from its surroundings. That way of living creates two problems, and the whole body of a fungus is the answer to them.

INTERACTIVE · ONE HYPHAL TIP IN DEAD WOOD

Release, digest, absorb, grow on

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
HYPHAHYPHAcellulose: too big
to absorbenzymes released
at the tipenzymes cut it
into glucosesmall molecules nowglucose is absorbedtaken in through
the wallthe tip grows onnext food
1 · ENZYMES OUT

The fungus releases digestive enzymes

Big molecules such as cellulose and starch cannot cross into a cell. So the hypha releases enzymes into whatever it is growing through. They are released at the growing tip.

2 · DIGESTION, OUTSIDE THE BODY

The enzymes break the food down

Out in the wood, the enzymes cut cellulose into single glucose molecules. This is extracellular digestion: digestion outside the cell.

3 · ABSORPTION

The small molecules are taken in

Glucose and other small molecules are absorbed straight across the wall and membrane. Feeding by absorbing dissolved molecules is called osmotrophy. A fungus digests first and takes the food in afterward.

4 · ON TO THE NEXT MEAL

It cannot walk, so it grows

A fungus has no way of moving. It finds food by growing. Where food is rich the hyphae grow fast and branch again and again. Where it is poor they slow down or stop.

TWO NAMES FOR WHAT YOU JUST WATCHED

Extracellular digestion and osmotrophy

EXTRACELLULAR DIGESTIONDigestion that happens outside the cell. The enzymes are released, and the food is broken down out in the wood or soil.
OSMOTROPHYFeeding by absorbing dissolved molecules across the cell surface. The opposite of swallowing food.
TOGETHERDigest first, take in afterward. An animal does it the other way round.

Said simply: fungi release digestive enzymes and then absorb nutrients.

TWO PROBLEMS, TWO ANSWERS

Why a fungus is built the way it is

PROBLEM 1 · FOOD IS TOO BIGLarge molecules cannot be absorbed. Answer: release enzymes that cut them small.
PROBLEM 2 · IT CANNOT MOVEAnimals go and look for food. A fungus cannot. Answer: grow toward it, as long thin hyphae.
WHAT IS ON THE MENU

Mostly dead plants

CELLULOSEThe main material of plant cell walls, and the most abundant biomolecule in and on soil. It is a chain of glucose, so it is rich in carbon and energy, but hard to break. Fungi release enzymes that can.
WOODIn wood, cellulose is bound up with lignin, which is even harder to break apart. Wood-rotting fungi are the specialists.
WHY FUNGI BEAT BACTERIA AT THISBacteria also digest with released enzymes, but they can barely move through soil and must wait for food to arrive. Hyphae grow out to find it, and can push into the inside of something as big as a tree trunk.
Check yourself: where does a fungus digest its food?

Outside its body. It releases digestive enzymes into its surroundings, the enzymes break large molecules into small ones, and the fungus absorbs those.

STEP 4 · THE WALL AND THE PUSH

Chitin: why a fungus has a tough wall

Every fungal cell is wrapped in a wall of chitin. The wall is not there only for protection. It is what lets a thread as thin as a hair force its way through soil and into wood.

INTERACTIVE · ONE HYPHA IN SOIL

Water in, pressure up, tip forward

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
chitin wallwater flows in (osmosis)more dissolved
molecules insidethe chitin wall holds: no burstingTURGORpressure pushes the tip forwardsoil
1 · OSMOSIS

Water flows into the hypha

The inside of a hypha holds more dissolved molecules than the dilute water in soil. So water flows in by osmosis.

2 · THE WALL

Chitin stops it from bursting

A cell with no wall would swell and burst. The chitin wall holds, so the water coming in builds up pressure instead. It is called turgor pressure.

3 · THE PUSH

Pressure drives the tip forward

A hypha grows only at its tip. Turgor pressure provides the force that pushes the tip on, through soil and into wood. That is how a fungus finds its food.

WHAT CHITIN IS

A sugar chain with nitrogen in it

WHAT KIND OF MOLECULEA complex carbohydrate: a modified polysaccharide that contains nitrogen.
WHERE ELSE YOU FIND ITThe exoskeleton of arthropods: insects, crabs, spiders.
WHAT IT GIVES THE WALLA wall that is strong but flexible. Strong enough to hold pressure, so the hypha can push.
DIAGRAM · THE SAME PRESSURE MOVES FOOD

Food taken up here can be used over there

food heremushroomfood carried inside the hyphae

Changes in pressure along the hyphae push water and dissolved food through them, much like sugar moving through a plant's phloem. It lets a fungus grow across a patch with no food, and build a mushroom above the ground.

Check yourself: why does a hypha need a strong cell wall to grow through soil?

Water flows in by osmosis. The chitin wall stops the hypha from bursting, so turgor pressure builds up, and that pressure is the force that pushes the tip forward.

STEP 5 · WHERE THE FUNGUS REALLY IS

The hidden forest

Ask someone to draw a fungus and they draw a mushroom. That is like drawing an apple and calling it the tree. Most of a fungus, and a surprising share of a whole forest, is underground.

INTERACTIVE · A FOREST, CUT AWAY

What is under the forest floor

Tap a button to explore
ABOVE GROUND · the small part you seeBELOW GROUNDMYCELIUM · all the hyphae togetherone hyphamushroomspuffballbracket fungi on
a living trunkspores
MYCELIUMThe body of the fungus is the networkAll the threads together are the mycelium (plural: mycelia). It runs through the soil, the leaf litter and the wood. This is the fungus. When you walk through a forest you are walking over an enormous amount of it.
ONE HYPHAA single threadOne thread is a hypha (plural: hyphae). Hyphae are 10 to 50 times thinner than a human hair. Being so long and thin gives them a huge surface for absorbing food.A hypha grows only at its tip, and it releases its digestive enzymes there. So growing forward is how a fungus both finds food and digests it.
FRUITING BODIESThe part you actually noticeA mushroom is a fruiting body. So is a white puffball, and so are the shelf-like brackets on a tree trunk. They are built by the mycelium for one job: making and releasing spores.Brackets on a standing tree are a sign that the fungus is already digesting its wood. Fungi do not wait for the tree to fall.
SPORESHow a fungus reproduces and spreadsSpores are tiny cells that rain out of the fruiting body and drift away on the air. One that lands on food can grow into a new mycelium. Spores are produced and dispersed during the fruiting-body stage of the life cycle.
TAP A BUTTON TO LIGHT UP ONE PARTThe mushroom is the tip of the icebergLook at how much of this picture is below the ground line. A mushroom is a small, short-lived part that a far bigger organism pushes up to release spores.
HOW MUCH FUNGUS IS THERE?

A lot, and mostly out of sight

Everything living below ground in a forest:
about 50% fungi
everything else

Much of the biomass of a forest ecosystem is underground, and about 50% of that is fungal tissue: mycelia. Fungi are common in forests, not rare.

THE FOUR WORDS

Name the parts

HYPHAEThe thin threads. One thread is a hypha.
MYCELIUMThe whole network of hyphae. Plural: mycelia.
FRUITING BODYThe part that produces and disperses spores. A mushroom or a puffball.
SPORESThe tiny reproductive cells it releases.
Check yourself: you pick every mushroom in a patch of forest. Have you removed the fungi?

No. You have removed some fruiting bodies. The mycelium that made them is still in the soil and the wood, and it is by far the larger part.

DIAGRAM · WHY THREADS AND NOT A LUMP

A huge surface for the size of the body

one lump:
little surfacethin threads: huge surfacesame amount of fungussame amount of fungus
WHAT THE SHAPE DOESA fungus feeds through its surface. Many long, thin hyphae give it an enormous surface area for its volume, so it can release enzymes and absorb food along all of it.
HOW THINHyphae are 10 to 50 times thinner than a human hair.
HOW BIG IT CAN GETOne mycelium of Armillaria ostoyae in Oregon covers more than 2,000 acres. Some fungi are the largest living organisms on Earth.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Hyphae

The thin threads that make up the body of a fungus. One thread is a hypha.

Mycelium

The whole network of hyphae. The plural is mycelia.

Fruiting body

The part of a fungus that produces and disperses spores. Mushrooms and puffballs are fruiting bodies.

Spores

The tiny reproductive cells a fungus releases from its fruiting body. Each one can grow into a new mycelium.

STEP 6 · HOW MANY, AND WHERE

Fungal function and diversity

Fungi are one of the most diverse groups of eukaryotes, and they do two big jobs in an ecosystem.

INTERACTIVE · SKETCH MAP · WHERE FUNGAL SPECIES ARE

Most diverse where it is wet

Tap a button to explore
0° · equatorfewer speciesmore specieswet tropics:
the mostdeserts: fewfewer toward the polesa sketch of the pattern, not measured values
NEAR THE EQUATOR, WHERE IT IS WETThe most species of fungiFungal diversity is greatest at the equator. The warmest colors sit over tropical rainforest: the Amazon basin, Central America, South-East Asia.The reason shows up in the next button: these are the places with the most rain.
DESERTSEven at low latitudes, few speciesThe Sahara and Arabia are not far from the equator, yet they have some of the lowest fungal diversity on the map. They are hot, but they are dry.So latitude alone is not the cause. The strongest predictor of fungal species richness is mean annual precipitation. Fungi need moisture.
TOWARD THE POLESA decline, but a gentle oneDiversity declines toward the poles. But it does not decline as sharply as plant species richness does. There are still plenty of fungal species in cool northern forests.
TAP A REGIONWhere on Earth are there the most kinds of fungi?Warm colors mean more species, cool colors mean fewer. All three patterns are showing now. Tap a button to pick one out.
DIVERSITY

The numbers and the pattern

HOW MANY SPECIESAn estimated 0.8 to 5.1 million worldwide.
WITH LATITUDEGreatest at the equator, declining toward the poles. The decline is less sharp than for plants.
STRONGEST PREDICTORMean annual precipitation.
ALSO IMPORTANTSoil properties, for example pH.
FUNCTION · TWO ROLES IN AN ECOSYSTEM

Decomposers and mutualists

DECOMPOSERSKey players in nutrient cycling. They break down dead matter, including wood, which almost nothing else can.
MUTUALISTSMany fungi live in a mutualism with plants. The next step is the most important example.
Check yourself: a hot desert and a rainforest sit at the same latitude. Which has more fungal species, and what does that tell you?

The rainforest. Same latitude, very different rainfall. It shows that precipitation, not distance from the equator by itself, is the strongest predictor.

DIAGRAM · CONNECTING THE DOTS

Why rain matters so much to a fungus

123water in the soil
1 · EATING HAPPENS IN WATERThe enzymes are released into the surroundings and the food comes back dissolved. Both need a film of water around the hypha.
2 · GROWING NEEDS WATERThe push at the tip is turgor pressure, and turgor pressure is water flowing in.
3 · TRANSPORT NEEDS WATERFood moves through the hyphae in flowing water.
SO THE PATTERN MAKES SENSE The strongest predictor of how many fungal species live in a place is mean annual precipitation. And decomposition speeds up where it is warm and moist. A body that eats, grows and moves food with water does best where there is water.

The map pattern is from Tedersoo et al. (2014), Nature. Soil properties such as pH matter too, so rain is the strongest factor, not the only one.

STEP 7 · FUNGI AS MUTUALISTS

Mycorrhizae: an extension of the root

Not every fungus lives on dead matter. Mycorrhizal fungi grow in and around the roots of living plants. The name means "fungus-root".

DIAGRAM · ONE ROOT AND ITS FUNGUS

The threads reach where the root cannot

PLANT · makes sugarsFUNGAL HYPHAE ↓what the root
reaches alonephosphate → plantsugars → fungusP = phosphate

The hyphae are far thinner than any root, and there are far more of them. They work as an extension of the root system, scavenging nutrients from soil the root would never touch.

WHO GETS WHAT

A trade

THE PLANT GETSHelp taking up nutrients, in particular phosphate.
THE FUNGUS GETSCarbohydrates: glucose and other sugars that the plant made by photosynthesis.
SO IT ISA mutualism: both gain. Module 2.1 has the full story.
HOW COMMON IS IT?

Most land plants have one

Each dot is 5% of land plant species. Filled: 85%. Ring: where "more than 90%" would reach.

Mycorrhizal fungi form these associations with 85% of land plant species. You will also see it given as more than 90% of land plants. Either way: nearly all of them.

Check yourself: a mycorrhizal fungus is a chemoheterotroph. Where is it getting its carbon?

From the plant, as sugars. It still takes in organic molecules made by another organism, which is what hetero means. It just gets them from a living plant instead of from detritus.

THREE REASONS THE THREADS BEAT THE ROOT

How the fungus gets what the root cannot

1 · REACHThe fungal network can stretch more than 10 cm beyond the root, so far more soil is within reach.
2 · THINNESSHyphae are so thin that they slip into tiny spaces between soil particles where no root fits.
3 · ENZYMESThe fungus releases enzymes that make nutrients in the soil easier to take up.
INTERACTIVE · TWO KINDS OF MYCORRHIZAE

Which one helps with phosphorus?

Tap the buttons, or The other kind, to click through all 2
a sheath around the root tipthreads between the root cellsnothing to see from outsidearbuscules: inside the root cells
ECTOMYCORRHIZAE

A coat around the root

A thick sheath of fungal cells surrounds the root tip, and threads grow between the root cells. This kind gives the plant access to nitrogen it could not otherwise reach.

ENDOMYCORRHIZAE

Branched inside the root cells

Nothing shows on the outside. The fungus grows into the root cells and branches into tree-shaped arbuscules, a huge surface for trading. This is the kind that matters most for phosphorus.

Both kinds also send a wide network of threads out into the soil.

NOT A GIFT · A TRADE THAT COSTS

Each partner is in it for itself

paid to the fungus: 4% to 20%kept by the plant

The plant pays for its fungus with 4% to 20% of all the carbohydrate it makes. That is a real cost.

poor soil: lots of fungusrich soil: very little

So the plant does not hand out sugar for nothing. Where the soil already supplies plenty of nutrients, as in a well-fertilized field, far fewer of its roots carry the fungus. In natural soils, nutrients are scarce, and mycorrhizal roots are the norm.

Neither side is being generous. The fungus takes sugars because it needs carbon. The plant gives them up because that is the price of phosphate.

REAL EXPERIMENTS · POTATOES, WITH AND WITHOUT ADDED FUNGUS

What the fungus is worth to the plant

no fungus added mycorrhizal fungus added
EXPERIMENT 1 · 231 FARM FIELDS
38.342.2no fungus addedfungus addedtons of potatoes per hectare

One mycorrhizal fungus was added to seed potatoes in 231 field trials across North America and Europe over four years. Fields with the fungus averaged 3.9 tons more per hectare, a gain of 9.5%.

Hijri (2016), Mycorrhiza 26: 209 to 214.

EXPERIMENT 2 · ONE FIELD, TWO KINDS OF FERTILIZER
100133100145chemical fertilizercomposttuber yield · no fungus added = 100

Potato plots were given mycorrhizal fungi or none. In the first year the plots with fungi yielded 33% more with chemical fertilizer and 45% more with compost. In the second year the gain was smaller, 10 to 20%.

Douds, Nagahashi, Reider and Hepperly (2007), Biological Agriculture and Horticulture 25: 67 to 78.

READ THE BARS CAREFULLYThe gray bars are not plants with no fungus at all. Field soil already has some. The comparison is extra fungus added against none added.
IT IS NOT ONLY PHOSPHATEThe second field was already very rich in phosphorus, and the potatoes still did better. Mycorrhizae can help in other ways too, such as making roots less open to infection.
IT DOES NOT ALWAYS WORKThe size of the gain changed from year to year, and in the same group's trials one potato variety did not respond at all.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Mycorrhizal fungi

Fungi that grow in and around plant roots and act as an extension of them. They help the plant take up phosphate and get sugars in return.

STEP 8 · DECOMPOSITION UNDER WATER

Whale falls: one carcass, a whole community

Everything so far has been on land. Decomposition happens in water too, with one main difference in what sets the speed.

INTERACTIVE · WHAT HAPPENS TO A DEAD WHALE

A whale fall, stage by stage

Tap the buttons, or Next stage, to click through all 4
sunlit surface · where the whale feddeep sea · cold, dark, little fooda whale dies
and sinksSTAGE 1 · the fleshhagfishsharkcrabsSTAGE 2 · the bonesSNOTWORMS
growing on the bonesBACTERIA
purple matsAFTERWARDS · open questionswhere do the young
snotworms go next?
THE FALLA whale dies near the surface and sinksThe whale spent its life feeding in the sunlit upper ocean. When it dies, all of that organic matter sinks to the sea floor, where food is scarce. The carcass links two biomes: matter made near the surface now feeds the deep.
STAGE 1 · SCAVENGERSFlesh-eating animals arrive firstOnce the carcass is on the bottom, mobile scavengers find it and eat the soft tissue: hagfish, sharks, crabs and other arthropods. They strip the flesh down to the skeleton.
STAGE 2 · THE SKELETONThen the bones are eaten tooWith the flesh gone, a different community takes over. Bacteria feed on what is left in and around the bones. Snotworms, bone-eating worms, grow on the skeleton itself.It is cold down here, and temperature is a key driver of decomposition in water, so this stage is slow.
AFTERWARDSA lot is still unknownA whale fall is a rare island of food in a huge, empty sea floor. Snotworms need bones to live on. So when one skeleton is used up, where do they go, and how do their young find the next one? Nobody is sure yet. Much about these communities is still being worked out.
DECOMPOSITION IN AQUATIC ENVIRONMENTS

Two things to know

TEMPERATURETemperature is a key driver of decomposition rates in water. Cold, deep water slows everything down.
CARCASSESCarcasses can link aquatic biomes and provide important resource inputs wherever they land.
WHO LIVES AT A WHALE FALL

The community, in order

1Scavengers
Animals that eat the flesh: fish such as hagfish and sharks, and arthropods such as crabs.
2Snotworms
Bone-eating worms that live on the skeleton.
3Bacteria
Decomposers that feed on the skeleton and on the enriched mud around it.
THEN AND NOW

There used to be far more whales

ONCE · for every whale alive todayat least 6and as many as 20TODAY1

Whale populations were once 6 to 20 times higher than they are now. Hunting removed most of them.

ZOOM OUT

What are the ecosystem impacts?

Far fewer whales alive means far fewer whales dying and sinking. So the deep sea now receives fewer whale falls than it once did.

For the communities that depend on them, that is less food and less habitat, spaced further apart. A change at the sunlit surface reaches all the way to the sea floor, because carcasses link the two.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Whale fall

A dead whale that has sunk to the sea floor, and the community of scavengers, worms and bacteria that lives on it.

Lock it in · Part 2

  1. A chemoheterotroph gets its energy and its carbon from organic molecules. Decomposers are chemoheterotrophs that feed on detritus.
  2. Decomposers are bacteria, archaea and fungi, plus a few other eukaryotes: all three domains.
  3. Fungi are eukaryotes, closely related to animals. They release enzymes, digest outside the body (extracellular digestion), and absorb the small molecules (osmotrophy).
  4. Their cell walls are chitin. Water flows in by osmosis, the wall holds, and the turgor pressure pushes the hyphal tip forward.
  5. Most fungi are multicellular: thin hyphae, with a huge surface for their volume, form a mycelium. The mushroom is only the fruiting body, which releases spores. Yeasts are the single-celled fungi.
  6. Much of a forest's biomass is underground, and about 50% of that is fungal tissue.
  7. There are an estimated 0.8 to 5.1 million fungal species. Diversity is greatest at the equator, and precipitation is the strongest predictor.
  8. Mycorrhizal fungi help plants take up phosphate and get sugars in return. It is a trade: it costs the plant 4% to 20% of its carbohydrate.
  9. In water, temperature is a key driver. A whale fall carries matter from the surface to the deep sea: scavengers first, then snotworms and bacteria on the bones.
MODULE 2.4 · PART 3

Nitrogen and phosphorus: following the atoms

THE QUESTION Air is mostly nitrogen. So why is nitrogen so often the thing plants run short of, and what happens when we give them too much?

Ten steps: what the two nutrients are for, how they move through a food web, pools and fluxes, the nitrogen cycle, who fixes nitrogen, denitrification, a practice trace, phosphorus, hippos, and dead zones.

STEP 1 · WHY THESE TWO ELEMENTS

What nitrogen and phosphorus are for

Parts 1 and 2 were about how nutrients get recycled, and who does it. This part follows two of the nutrients. Start with why every organism needs them.

NNEEDED TO BUILDNitrogen
ProteinsNucleic acids

Every amino acid has nitrogen in it, so every protein does. So do DNA and RNA.

PNEEDED TO BUILDPhosphorus
ATPNucleic acidsPhospholipids

Phospholipids are what cell membranes are built from. Phosphorus is essential for all life forms.

DIAGRAM · A PRODUCER TAKING UP NUTRIENTS

Producers take them up as simple ions

NH₄⁺NO₃⁻PO₄³⁻ammoniumnitratephosphatebuilt into proteins,
nucleic acids, ATP,
membranesINORGANIC IN THE SOILORGANIC IN THE PLANT
NITROGEN PRODUCERS CAN USEAmmonium (NH₄⁺) and nitrate (NO₃⁻).
PHOSPHORUS PRODUCERS CAN USEPhosphate. Land plants get it from the soil. Aquatic producers get it from the water.
THENThe atoms are built into organic molecules. Taking a nutrient up and building it in is assimilation.
INTERACTIVE · FIVE MOLECULES, WITH N AND P MARKED

See where the nitrogen and the phosphorus actually sit

Tap the buttons, or Next molecule, to click through all 5
PROTEIN · a chain of amino acidsa nitrogen in every amino acidgray box = the side group that differsNUCLEOTIDE · the unit of DNA and RNAphosphate
groupsugarbase
has nitrogenATP · the cell's energy carrierbase
has nitrogensugarthree phosphate
groupsPHOSPHOLIPID · phospho + lipidphosphate
headtwo fatty
tails: the
lipid parta cell membrane: two layers of themCARBOHYDRATE · a sugarcarbon, hydrogen and oxygen only: no N, no P
PROTEIN · NEEDS NITROGENNitrogen in every amino acidA protein is a chain of amino acids. Each amino acid begins with a nitrogen atom, so a protein is full of nitrogen. No phosphorus in the chain itself.
NUCLEIC ACIDS · NEED BOTHPhosphorus in the backbone, nitrogen in the basesDNA and RNA are chains of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has a phosphate group (phosphorus), a sugar, and a base (the bases are rings that contain nitrogen). So nucleic acids need both N and P.
ATP · NEEDS BOTHThree phosphates on a nucleotideATP is a nucleotide with three phosphate groups in a row. That is where the name comes from: adenosine triphosphate. Its base, adenine, contains nitrogen. Every cell makes and spends ATP constantly.
PHOSPHOLIPID · NEEDS PHOSPHORUSThe main use of phosphorus in a cellRead the word in two halves: phospho + lipid. A phosphate head on two fatty tails. It belongs to the class of molecules called lipids, or fats. Every cell membrane is a double layer of phospholipids, so every cell needs a great deal of them.
CARBOHYDRATE · NEEDS NEITHERJust carbon, hydrogen and oxygenSugars, starch and cellulose contain no nitrogen and no phosphorus. That is why a producer can make sugar from CO₂ and water alone, but cannot grow without taking up N and P as well.
THE BIG MOLECULES OF LIFE

Which need N, which need P

PROTEINSNitrogen. In every amino acid.
NUCLEIC ACIDS · DNA AND RNANitrogen and phosphorus. N in the bases, P in the backbone.
ATPNitrogen and phosphorus. Three phosphate groups.
LIPIDSOrdinary fats contain neither. The critical exception is the phospholipids: phosphorus. They are the main use of phosphorus in a cell.
CARBOHYDRATESNeither. Only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
Check yourself: a plant has plenty of light, water and CO₂ but no phosphate at all. Which molecules can it not make?

Nucleic acids, ATP and phospholipids. So it cannot copy its DNA, cannot carry energy around its cells, and cannot build membranes for new cells. It can still make sugar, which needs no phosphorus, but it cannot grow.

AND HETEROTROPHS? They need nitrogen and phosphorus for exactly the same molecules. They just cannot take up the ions. A heterotroph gets its N and P atoms from its food.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Assimilation

Taking up an inorganic nutrient and building its atoms into organic molecules. Producers assimilate ammonium and nitrate.

STEP 2 · UP THE FOOD CHAIN AND BACK

How N and P move through a food web

The same four moves carry nitrogen and phosphorus around every ecosystem. This is the giraffe and the leaf from Part 1, drawn as a loop.

DIAGRAM · ONE LOOP, FOUR MOVES

Taken up, eaten, shed, released

ProducersConsumersDetritusInorganic nutrientsuptake +
assimilationeatendeath
and wastedecompositionORGANIC · N and P inside proteins, DNA, ATPINORGANIC

Follow the arrows clockwise from the bottom left. The atom goes inorganic → organic once, at the producer, and organic → inorganic once, at the decomposers. In between it is only passed along.

THE FOUR MOVES

What happens at each arrow

1Uptake and assimilation
A producer takes up ammonium, nitrate or phosphate and builds the atoms into its own proteins, nucleic acids, ATP and phospholipids.
2Eaten
A consumer eats the producer, digests those molecules, and rebuilds the atoms into its own. The same again at each step up the chain.
3Death and waste
Everything that dies, and everything that is excreted, joins the detritus. The N and P are still in organic molecules.
4Decomposition
Decomposers break those molecules down and release the N and P in inorganic form. Ready for step 1 again.
WHAT "RECYCLED" MEANS Decomposers are the recyclers. To say a nutrient is recycled is to say the same atoms are released from dead matter and taken up by producers again, over and over.
INTERACTIVE · FOLLOW AN ATOM AROUND THE LOOP

Consumption carries N and P up. Decomposition brings them back.

Tap Next move to go through all 5
NH₄⁺ NO₃⁻ PO₄³⁻SOILPRODUCERHERBIVOREPREDATORDETRITUSDECOMPOSERSuptake +
assimilationherbivorypredationdeath
and wastedecomposition
1 · UPTAKE AND ASSIMILATIONInorganic in the soil → organic in a producerUptake: the roots take in ammonium, nitrate and phosphate ions. Assimilation: the plant builds those atoms into its own organic molecules: proteins, nucleic acids, ATP, phospholipids. This is the only place where N and P go from inorganic to organic.
2 · CONSUMPTION: HERBIVORYA consumer eats a producerConsumption is eating. When the food is a producer it is called herbivory. Then digestion: the giraffe breaks the plant's big molecules into small ones (proteins into amino acids). Then biosynthesis: it builds its own molecules from them.
3 · CONSUMPTION: PREDATIONA consumer eats a consumerWhen the food is another animal, consumption is called predation. The steps inside are the same: digest the prey's molecules, rebuild them as your own. N and P move up the food chain by consumption, one level at a time, always inside organic molecules.
4 · DEATH AND WASTEEverything ends up as detritusWhatever dies without being eaten, and everything that is excreted, joins the detritus. The nitrogen and phosphorus are still locked in organic molecules, which producers cannot take up.
5 · DECOMPOSITIONOrganic → inorganic, and the loop closesDecomposers break the organic molecules down and release the atoms in inorganic form: ammonium (some of which other microbes turn into nitrate) and phosphate. Those are available to primary producers again. Back to step 1.
THREE WORDS TO KEEP STRAIGHT

Consumption, digestion, assimilation

CONSUMPTIONEating. It is how N and P move up a food chain. Eating a producer is herbivory. Eating another animal is predation.
DIGESTIONTaking the food apart. Large organic molecules are broken into small ones: proteins into amino acids, nucleic acids into nucleotides.
ASSIMILATIONBuilding a nutrient into your own organic molecules. In a nutrient cycle the word is used for producers: after uptake of the inorganic ion comes assimilation into protein, DNA and the rest.
ONE WORD, TWO MODULES In Module 2.3, "assimilated" described the share of its food that a consumer absorbs. It is the same idea here: assimilation always means taken in and made part of the body.
STEP 3 · THE VOCABULARY OF A CYCLE

Pools and fluxes

Every biogeochemical cycle is described with two words. One is for where the element is. The other is for the element moving.

TWO WORDS

A place, and a movement

POOLPOOLFLUXsoilplantsan amountan amountan amount
per year
POOL · A NOUN, A PLACEWhere the element is held: the atmosphere, the soil, the water, living things, detritus. Reservoir and compartment mean the same thing.
FLUX · A VERB, A MOVEMENTThe element moving from one pool to another. Fluxes are the arrows in a cycle diagram, and they are rates: an amount per year.
TRY IT · POOL OR FLUX? TAP TO CHECK

Sort these eight

Detritus

POOL. Dead matter is a place where nitrogen sits. This is the one people get wrong.

Assimilation

FLUX. Nitrogen moving from soil or water into a producer.

The atmosphere

POOL. It holds N₂ gas.

Denitrification

FLUX. Nitrogen moving from nitrate back to the air.

Soil

POOL. It holds ammonium and nitrate.

Nitrogen fixation

FLUX. Nitrogen moving out of the air into a usable form.

Plants

POOL. Their tissues hold nitrogen.

Decomposition

THE POOLSWhere the nitrogen isEach box is a pool with the amount it holds. The atmosphere dwarfs everything else. Vegetation and marine life, the living pools, are tiny by comparison. You do not need to memorize the numbers, only which is biggest.
FLUX · NATURAL NITROGEN FIXATIONOut of the air, by microbesBacteria and archaea on land and in the ocean pull N₂ out of the atmosphere and turn it into forms living things can use. This is the main natural way nitrogen enters ecosystems.
FLUX · HUMAN NITROGEN FIXATIONOut of the air, by usFactories fix nitrogen to make fertilizer, and farmers plant crops such as soybeans whose root bacteria fix nitrogen. Compare the numbers with the last step: human fixation is now about as large as natural fixation on land.
FLUX · DENITRIFICATIONBack into the airOther microbes turn nitrate back into N₂ gas, which returns to the atmosphere. Rivers also carry nitrogen from the land pool to the ocean pool: that is a flux too.

Numbers are from the published global figure. They are there to compare sizes, not to memorize.

START BIG, THEN ZOOM IN

How to read the global picture

FOUR PLACES TO LOOKThe atmosphere, the land (plants and soil), the water, and the rock. Microbes are everywhere in between, moving nitrogen from one to the next.
THE KEY FLUXESNitrogen fixation, which has three kinds: natural biological, lightning, and industrial. And denitrification, which sends it back.
WHAT PRODUCERS CAN USEOnly two forms out of all of this: ammonium (NH₄⁺) and nitrate (NO₃⁻).
Check yourself: hippos carry nitrogen from grassland into a river. Is that a pool or a flux?

A flux. The grassland and the river are pools. The nitrogen moving from one to the other, inside the hippo, is a flux. Step 9 is about exactly this.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Pool

A place where an element is held: the atmosphere, soil, water, or living things. Also called a reservoir or a compartment.

Reservoir

Another word for a pool.

Flux

The movement of an element from one pool to another.

STEP 4 · THE MAIN EVENT

The nitrogen cycle

Now put the pools and the fluxes together. Nitrogen starts in the air as N₂ gas, gets pulled into living things by microbes, moves through the food web, and is returned by microbes.

EVERY STEP, EVERY FORM · THE WHOLE NITROGEN CYCLE ON ONE CARD

Eight arrows. Follow one nitrogen atom all the way round

Every form of nitrogen is a stop on the map. Every step is a numbered arrow, and the list under the map uses the same numbers and colors. The drawings further down take the steps one at a time, in these same colors.

THE THREE THINGS TO NEVER MIX UP Producers can take up only ammonium and nitrate. Fixation brings nitrogen in from the air and denitrification sends it back. Nitrification does neither: it only changes ammonium into nitrate.

N₂ gasammonia (NH₃)
Who does it: microbes: some bacteria and some archaea.This is how nitrogen enters the living world. In water, ammonia picks up a hydrogen and becomes ammonium (NH₄⁺), a form producers can take up.
FLUX 2 · NITRIFICATIONAmmonia becomes nitrate
ammonia (NH₃)nitrate (NO₃⁻)
Who does it: microbes in soil and water. They get their energy from the reaction.Nitrate is the other form producers can take up. So after this step there are two usable forms: ammonium and nitrate.
FLUX 3 · UPTAKE AND ASSIMILATIONInto a producer, and into its molecules
NH₄⁺ and NO₃⁻proteins, nucleic acids
Who does it: primary producers.The producer takes up the inorganic nitrogen and builds the atoms into organic molecules (biosynthesis). This is where nitrogen goes from inorganic to organic.
FLUX 4 · FEEDINGUp the food chain
producer's moleculesconsumer's molecules
Who does it: consumers.Consumers obtain nitrogen from their food. They digest the proteins they eat into amino acids and rebuild them as their own.
FLUX 5 · DECOMPOSITIONBack out of dead matter
detritusammonia (NH₃)
Who does it: microbes: the decomposers.Dead producers, dead consumers and their waste all become detritus. Decomposers break the organic molecules down and return the nitrogen as ammonia. This is where nitrogen goes from organic to inorganic.
FLUX 6 · DENITRIFICATIONBack to the air
nitrate (NO₃⁻)N₂ gas
Who does it: microbes living where there is little or no oxygen.They use nitrate in their respiration, and it leaves as N₂ gas. This returns nitrogen to the atmosphere and removes usable nitrogen from the soil or water.

THE PROBLEM · A TRIPLE BONDWhy the biggest pool is out of reachIn N₂ gas the two nitrogen atoms share three bonds. A triple bond is extremely stable, so it takes a great deal of energy to pull the atoms apart. Plants, animals and fungi have no way of doing it. That is why air that is 78% nitrogen cannot feed a plant.
NITROGEN FIXATIONBreak the bond, add hydrogensNitrogen-fixing bacteria and archaea have an enzyme, nitrogenase, that can break the triple bond. As the atoms come apart, hydrogens are added to each one, giving two molecules of ammonia, NH₃.Where the hydrogen comes from: hydrogen ions (H⁺) that are always present in the watery inside of the cell, plus electrons (e⁻) that the bacterium takes from its food. An H⁺ and an electron together make one hydrogen atom. The reaction is costly: the cell spends a lot of ATP on it.
AMMONIA BECOMES AMMONIUMOne more hydrogen, from waterAmmonia dissolves in the water in soil, lakes and the sea, and picks up a hydrogen ion from the water. It is now ammonium, NH₄⁺. So NH₃ and NH₄⁺ are the same nitrogen, one hydrogen apart, and in wet places you mostly find ammonium.
NITRIFICATIONAmmonium is switched to nitrateNitrifying bacteria and archaea take the hydrogens off the nitrogen and put oxygens on instead: first nitrite (NO₂⁻), then nitrate (NO₃⁻). They do it to get energy, and they use oxygen gas to do it. Overall: NH₄⁺ + 2 O₂ → NO₃⁻ + H₂O + 2 H⁺.
DENITRIFICATIONThe reverse trip, back to N₂Where there is no oxygen gas, such as waterlogged soil, some bacteria use the oxygen in nitrate for their respiration instead. The oxygens are stripped off, the nitrogen atoms pair up again, and N₂ gas escapes to the air. Usable nitrogen has been lost from the soil.

N₂NH₃NH₄⁺NO₃⁻rootcannot be taken up+ waternitrificationgasammoniaammoniumnitrate
N₂ · NITROGEN GASNot taken up. The triple bond is the problem.

take them updecomposersdead matter
and wasteno O₂DENITRIFICATION · NO₃⁻ → N₂waterlogged
NITROGEN FIXATION · N₂ → NH₃Four routes down from the airRhizobium in the root nodules of legumes. Free-living bacteria and archaea in the soil. Trichodesmium, a cyanobacterium, in the ocean. And lightning, the one route that is not biological. All of them turn N₂ gas into a form that ends up in soil or water.
NITRIFICATION · NH₃ → NO₃⁻In the soil and in waterNitrifying microbes turn ammonia into nitrate. It happens wherever there is ammonia and oxygen, on land and in water, which is why nitrate is the most common usable form in both.
UPTAKE AND ASSIMILATIONTwo forms, two kinds of producerOn land, plant roots take up ammonium and nitrate from the soil. In water, phytoplankton take the same two ions straight from the water around them. No roots are needed: the nutrients come in across the surface of each cell.Either way, the producer then assimilates the nitrogen: it builds it into amino acids, proteins and nucleic acids.
DECOMPOSITION · ORGANIC N → NH₃At the surface and in the soilDead leaves, dead animals and dung are broken down by decomposers, which return the nitrogen to the soil as ammonia. In water, dead cells sink and are decomposed on the way down and on the bottom.
DENITRIFICATION · NO₃⁻ → N₂The reverse of fixation, in airless placesIn waterlogged soil and other places with no oxygen, denitrifying bacteria use nitrate in their respiration and release N₂ gas. This is the arrow that returns nitrogen to the atmosphere and closes the whole cycle.
LAND AND WATER

The same cycle in two settings

FIXATIONLand: Rhizobium in legume nodules, free-living soil microbes. Ocean: Trichodesmium. Everywhere: lightning.
UPTAKELand: through roots, from the soil. Water: straight into phytoplankton cells, from the water around them.
ASSIMILATIONThe same in both: the producer builds the nitrogen into amino acids, proteins and nucleic acids.
DENITRIFICATIONWherever there is nitrate but no oxygen: waterlogged soil, and oxygen-poor water and mud.
Check yourself: which two fluxes are opposites of each other?

Nitrogen fixation and denitrification. Fixation takes N₂ out of the air and makes it usable. Denitrification takes usable nitrate and sends it back to the air as N₂.

NOTICE WHO DOES THE WORK

Microbes run four of the six fluxes

BY MICROBESNitrogen fixation, nitrification, decomposition, denitrification.
BY PRODUCERSUptake and assimilation.
BY CONSUMERSFeeding.

Take away bacteria and archaea and the cycle stops at both ends: nothing brings nitrogen in, and nothing returns it.

TWO WAYS IN, ONE WAY OUT

In and out of the usable pool

ADDS USABLE NITROGENNitrogen fixation, from the air. Decomposition, from dead matter.
REMOVES USABLE NITROGENDenitrification, back to the air.
Go deeper: one more flux in the full diagram
Textbook versions of the cycle add anammox. Some bacteria combine ammonia with nitrite (NO₂⁻, the halfway point of nitrification) and release N₂ gas. Like denitrification, it sends nitrogen back to the atmosphere.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Nitrogen fixation

Turning N₂ gas into ammonia, a form living things can use. Only some bacteria and archaea can do it.

STEP 5 · THE WAY IN

Who fixes nitrogen, and how much

Nitrogen fixation is the only door from the huge atmospheric pool into the living world. Only prokaryotes can open it.

DIAGRAM · A LEGUME ROOT

Rhizobium: nitrogen fixers in root nodules

N₂ from the airNODULE
Rhizobium insideNH₄⁺ upsugars
down
WHORhizobium, bacteria that live as mutualists inside nodules on the roots of legumes (peas, beans, soybeans, clover).
DOMAINBacteria.
WHAT THEY DOTake N₂ from the atmospheric reservoir, carry out nitrogen fixation, and produce NH₄⁺, which the plant can use.
WHAT THEY GETSugars and a home. Module 2.1 covers this mutualism.
WHICH DOMAINS CAN FIX NITROGEN?

Bacteria and Archaea only

BACTERIA✓ Some
ARCHAEA✓ Some
EUKARYA✕ None

Rhizobium is not the only one. Free-living bacteria fix nitrogen in soil, Trichodesmium does it in the ocean, and some archaea do too. No plant or animal can do it by itself.

CHART · SOURCES OF FIXED NITROGEN PER YEAR, RELATIVE

Natural sources vs. human sources

Natural · about 150
Biological fixationLightning
Human · about 140
Nitrogen fertilizer, made industriallyNitrogen-fixing cropsFossil fuels

Two natural kinds: biological fixation and lightning. Biological fixation is far more common.

"Nitrogen-fixing crops" are legumes such as soybeans. The plants do not fix nitrogen themselves: the Rhizobium bacteria in their root nodules do.

Human sources now add almost as much as all natural sources put together. Every one of them enters the cycle at the same place: the nitrogen fixation arrow, turning N₂ into usable nitrogen.

Values are read from the published chart, on its own scale.

SCENE · THE ONE NATURAL ROUTE THAT IS NOT ALIVE

Lightning fixes nitrogen too

N₂ + O₂NO₃⁻ · nitrateLIGHTNING
energy to break
the triple bondrain carries it downroots take it up
HOW LIGHTNING DOES IT

Raw energy instead of an enzyme

1The strike
A lightning bolt is hot enough to break the triple bond in N₂, and the bond in O₂, in the air around it.
2New molecules
The freed nitrogen and oxygen atoms join into nitrogen oxides.
3Rain
These dissolve in rain and reach the ground as nitrate, a form roots can take up.
KEEP IT IN PROPORTION On the chart above, lightning is the thin slice at the top of the natural bar. Biological fixation is far more common. The two natural kinds of nitrogen fixation are biological fixation and lightning.
Check yourself: fill in the blanks. The ___ mutualists live inside nodules on plant roots. They are ___ (domain), take nitrogen from the ___ reservoir, do ___ (process), and produce ___.

Rhizobium. Bacteria. The atmospheric reservoir. Nitrogen fixation. NH₄⁺ (ammonium).

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Rhizobium bacteria

Nitrogen-fixing bacteria that live in nodules on the roots of legumes.

STEP 6 · THE WAY OUT

Denitrification: usable nitrogen goes back to the air

Fixation is the door in. Denitrification is the door out. Where there is no oxygen, microbes turn nitrate back into N₂ gas, and that nitrogen is out of reach again.

THE ONE-LINE VERSION

Nitrate in, nitrogen gas out

NO₃⁻ nitrate→ denitrifying microbes, no O₂ →N₂ gas
WHAT GOES INNitrate, NO₃⁻. One of the two forms producers can take up.
WHAT COMES OUTN₂ gas, which returns to the atmosphere. Producers cannot use it.
WHO DOES ITMicrobes. Denitrifying bacteria, and some archaea.
WHEREOnly where there is no oxygen: waterlogged soil, the mud under a lake, oxygen-poor water.
INTERACTIVE · SAME SOIL, TWO CONDITIONS

Take the oxygen away and watch the nitrate

Tap the buttons, or Flood the soil, to click through all 2
NO₃⁻microbeO₂ in the
soil poresnitrate stays
for the rootsflooded:
no O₂N₂ gas escapesnitrate leaves

WITH OXYGEN

Nothing is lost

The spaces between soil grains hold air. Microbes respire with oxygen, as most organisms do. Nitrate stays in the soil, and roots take it up.

NO OXYGEN

Nitrate is used in place of oxygen

Water has filled the spaces, and the oxygen is used up. Denitrifying microbes switch to nitrate for their respiration. The nitrogen comes out as N₂ gas and bubbles away. The soil now holds less usable nitrogen.

DIAGRAM · WHY A MICROBE WOULD DO THIS

It is how they respire without oxygen

MOST ORGANISMSDENITRIFIERSO₂H₂ONO₃⁻N₂respirationrespiration

Respiration needs something to hand electrons to at the end. Most organisms use oxygen. Denitrifiers use nitrate in its place. This is anaerobic respiration.

So the microbe is not trying to remove nitrogen. Losing it to the air is a side effect of how the microbe gets its energy.

DIAGRAM · IN AND OUT

Why fixation can never stop

AIR · N₂ gasNH₄⁺ and NO₃⁻usable nitrogen in soil and waterfixation
INdenitrification
OUT

Denitrification is very good at sending nitrogen back to the air. If fixation stopped, the usable nitrogen would slowly run down, and primary production would run down with it.

Anammox is a second, smaller drain: some microbes in oxygen-poor water combine ammonium with nitrite and release N₂.

SIDE BY SIDE · THE TWO DOORS

Fixation and denitrification are opposites

FIXATIONDENITRIFICATION
DIRECTIONAir → living worldLiving world → air
FORMSN₂ → NH₃NO₃⁻ → N₂
WHOSome bacteria and archaeaSome bacteria and archaea
ENERGYCosts the cell a lot of ATPGives the cell energy: it is respiration
USABLE NITROGENGoes upGoes down
WORLDWIDE, PER YEARLand 128, ocean 120, by microbesLand 158, ocean 110

The last row is in teragrams of nitrogen per year, from the global nitrogen cycle figure in Cain et al., Ecology (2008), Figure 24.6. No need to memorize the numbers. The point is that the way out is about as big as the natural way in.

DO NOT MIX UP Denitrification removes usable nitrogen: nitrate to N₂ gas. Nitrification only changes one usable form into another: ammonium to nitrate. The names are close. The jobs are not.
Check yourself: a farm field floods and stays under water for two weeks. What happens to the nitrate in its soil, and why?

The water fills the spaces in the soil, and the oxygen there is used up. Denitrifying microbes then use nitrate for their respiration in place of oxygen. The nitrogen leaves as N₂ gas, so the soil ends up with less usable nitrogen for the crop.

Check yourself: is denitrification a pool or a flux?

A flux. It moves nitrogen from one pool (nitrate in soil or water) to another (N₂ in the atmosphere).

STEP 7 · PRACTICE

Trace one nitrogen atom

A standard exam task: follow a single atom from one organism to another, naming every process and the kind of molecule it is in at each stop. Try this one in an Antarctic food web.

MOVE 1 · DEATH AND WASTEFrom the seal into the detritusThe nitrogen atom starts inside an organic molecule in the seal, such as a protein. When the seal dies, or in its waste, that molecule joins the detritus.Molecule now: still organic. Seal protein, now dead matter.
MOVE 2 · DECOMPOSITIONDecomposers release itBacteria and archaea break the organic molecules down and release the nitrogen as ammonia, which becomes ammonium in the water.Molecule now: inorganic. NH₄⁺, dissolved in sea water.

Whale protein.Why this is the shortest path: nothing eats an elephant seal and is then eaten by a baleen whale, so the atom has to go down through the decomposers and back up through the producers.
THE FOOD WEB YOU NEED

Who eats whom here

PhytoplanktonKrillBaleen whale

Phytoplankton are the producers. Krill eat phytoplankton. Baleen whales eat krill. Elephant seals feed higher up, on fish and squid, and no path of feeding arrows leads from a seal to a baleen whale.

HOW TO ANSWER ANY QUESTION LIKE THIS 1. Can you get there by feeding arrows alone? If not, the atom must go through decomposition and back up from a producer. 2. Name each process. 3. At each stop say whether the atom is in an organic molecule or an inorganic one.
