ONE NITROGEN ATOMAir → soil → plant → animal → detritus → soil → airFixation brings it out of the air. A plant takes it up and assimilates it into protein. An animal gets it by consumption, digests the protein, and rebuilds its own. After death, decomposition releases it as ammonium. From there it is either taken up again, which is the short loop most atoms follow many times, or denitrified back to the air.
ONE PHOSPHORUS ATOMRock → soil → plant → animal → detritus → soilThere is no gas stop. Weathering slowly releases phosphate from rock into soil. A plant takes it up and assimilates it into DNA, ATP and phospholipids. Consumption and digestion pass it up the food chain. Decomposition returns it as phosphate, and the fast loop repeats. Some washes to the sea, sinks into sediment, and takes an enormously long time to become rock on land again.
ONE CARBON ATOMAir → plant → animal → detritus → decomposer → airPhotosynthesis takes it from CO₂ into a sugar. The plant builds the sugar into other molecules. An animal eats and digests them. At every stop, cellular respiration can send the atom straight back to the air as CO₂, and decomposers send back whatever is left. Module 2.5 follows carbon in full.
WHAT TO WATCH FOR

The same four moves every time

INTO LIFEUptake and assimilation by a producer (for carbon: photosynthesis). Inorganic becomes organic.
UP THE CHAINConsumption, then digestion, then rebuilding. Organic stays organic.
OUT OF LIFEDeath and waste: into the detritus.
BACK TO THE STARTDecomposition. Organic becomes inorganic again.
WHAT DIFFERS BETWEEN THE THREE Only the non-living stop. Nitrogen and carbon have a gas in the air. Phosphorus has none: it starts in rock, which is why its full cycle is so slow.
STEP 8 · THE OTHER NUTRIENT

The phosphorus cycle

Phosphorus moves through pools just as nitrogen does, but it starts somewhere very different, and part of its journey is extremely slow.

EVERY STEP · THE WHOLE PHOSPHORUS CYCLE ON ONE CARD

Rock to rock: eight arrows, one usable form, and no gas

Phosphorus is simpler than nitrogen. Most of it is in rock, not in the air. Producers use one form, the phosphate ion, PO₄³⁻. No microbe has to change it into another form first.

ROCKPO₄³⁻ in soilSEASEDIMENT12345678
1Weathering
phosphate locked in rock→PO₄³⁻ in soil and water
PHOSPHORUS ENTERS THE FOOD WEBWho: no organism. Rock breaks down chemically.Speed: slow.
2Uptake and assimilation
PO₄³⁻ in soil, or in the water column→ATP, nucleic acids, phospholipids
INORGANIC → ORGANICWho: primary producers. On land, mycorrhizal fungi help. In water, it comes from the water column.Speed: fast.
3Feeding
producer's molecules→consumer's molecules
Who: consumers. Their P atoms come from food.Speed: fast.
4Decomposition
detritus→PO₄³⁻
ORGANIC → INORGANICWho: decomposers. Some phosphate is taken straight back up. Some is carried away by water.Speed: fast.
5Runoff
PO₄³⁻ in soil→rivers, lakes, the sea
Who: no organism. Water carries it. Fertilizer washed off fields adds more and drives eutrophication.Speed: slow.
6The same fast loop, in the water
PO₄³⁻ in the water column→producers→consumers→decomposers
Who: phytoplankton, their consumers, and decomposers, in sunlit water. Upwelling can bring phosphate back up from deep water.Speed: fast.
7Sedimentation
phosphorus in the sea→sediment on the sea floor
PHOSPHORUS LEAVES THE FOOD WEBWho: no organism. What sinks builds up on the sea floor.Speed: very slow.
8Tectonic uplift
sediment→rock in mountains
Who: no organism. Sediments are raised into mountains, and weathering can start again.Speed: the slowest step of all.
FAST INSIDE, SLOW OUTSIDE Arrows 2, 3, 4 and 6 are the fast loops: phosphate moves quickly through plants and animals. Arrows 1, 5, 7 and 8 move phosphorus through soil, ocean and rock, and they are very slow. That is what slows the whole cycle.
THREE WAYS IT DIFFERS FROM NITROGEN The big pool is rock, not the atmosphere. There is one usable form, not two. And no step needs a microbe to change the form: phosphate is only passed along, taken up, eaten and released.

very slowSEDIMENTfungal

FASTPhosphate moves quickly through plants and animals: taken up, eaten, returned in waste and dead matter, taken up again.
SLOWThe processes that move phosphorus through the soil or the ocean are very slow. That is what slows the whole cycle down.
WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT PHOSPHORUS

The essentials

THE FORM PRODUCERS USEPhosphate. From the soil on land, from the water column in aquatic systems.
WHY EVERYTHING NEEDS ITTo make ATP, nucleic acids and phospholipids. Heterotrophs get their P atoms from food.
WHO HELPS PLANTS GET ITMycorrhizal fungi. Their threads reach phosphate far beyond the roots.
TOO MUCH OF ITExcess phosphorus in water drives eutrophication. Step 10 shows how.
SIDE BY SIDE

Nitrogen vs. phosphorus

NITROGENPHOSPHORUS
USABLE FORMAmmonium, nitratePhosphate
BUILDSProteins, nucleic acidsATP, nucleic acids, phospholipids
PARTNERRhizobium (bacteria)Mycorrhizal fungi
GAS IN THE AIR?Yes. N₂ is the largest pool.No gas form to speak of. It comes from rock and soil.

STEP 9 · ANIMALS MOVE NUTRIENTS TOO

Hippos: a conveyor belt from land to water

Nutrients do not only cycle on the spot. Animals can carry them from one ecosystem into another. Hippos in the Mara River in Kenya are the classic case.

SCENE · ONE HIPPO, ONE DAY

Eat on land, release in the river

NIGHT · grazes on landDAY · rests in the riverC, N and Pdung and urine
fertilize the watergrass is eaten here

Hippos graze on grassland at night and spend the day in the water, where they release dung and urine. Every day they move carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus from the terrestrial system into the freshwater one. Rainfall, runoff and gravity usually do this job. Here an animal does.

IN THE RIVER · THE DRY SEASON

How many hippos changes the answer

A FEW HIPPOSTheir nutrients act as fertilizer. Aquatic primary producers get more nitrogen and phosphorus, so NPP goes up.
A LOT OF HIPPOSToo much dung collects in slow, shallow water. The water turns murky, decomposers working on the dung use up the oxygen, fish die, and NPP goes down.

A hippo pool can go from clear to opaque in less than a day.

ON THE GRASSLAND

They change the land as well

Where hippos graze, the grass becomes stubbier and leafier, which makes it more nutritious for other grazers.

THE IDEA TO KEEP Ecosystems are linked. A nutrient flux can cross from land to water inside an animal, and whether it helps or harms depends on how much arrives.
INTERACTIVE · THE SAME POOL, FEW HIPPOS OR MANY

When fertilizer becomes too much

Tap the buttons, or Add more hippos, to click through all 2
O₂A FEW HIPPOSa little dung = fertilizermore algae · NPP goes UPMANY HIPPOSfar too much dungdecomposers use up the O₂fish die · NPP goes DOWN
DRY SEASON · A FEW HIPPOSA helpful dose of fertilizerThe dung and urine bring nitrogen and phosphorus that the river's producers were short of. Algae grow faster, so net primary productivity goes up, and there is more food for the whole aquatic food web.
DRY SEASON · MANY HIPPOSToo much of a good thingIn the dry season the river is low and slow, so dung piles up instead of washing away. It is a huge load of detritus. Decomposers multiply to break it down, and their respiration uses up the oxygen in the water. Fish die, the water turns murky, and productivity falls.This is the idea to hold on to for the rest of the module: a burst of decomposition strips oxygen out of water.
INTERACTIVE · ECOSYSTEM ENGINEERS

How hippos tie the grassland and the river together

Tap a button to explore
tall grassHIPPO LAWNshort, leafy,
more nutritiousother grazers
benefitdung → algae and microbesinvertebrates → fish → eagleeaglebirddragonfly
ON LAND · HIPPO LAWNSGrazing changes the grassWhere hippos graze night after night, the grass is kept closely cropped. It grows back stubbier and leafier, which makes it more nutritious. Other herbivores benefit from these lawns.
IN THE WATER · DUNGFertilizer, and foodDung is a fertilizer for algae and microbes, and it is food for scavenger fish. Nitrogen and phosphorus that were in grass on land are now in the river: a flux from the terrestrial system to the freshwater one.
UP THE AQUATIC FOOD WEBThe nutrients keep movingMicroorganisms are food for aquatic invertebrates. Predatory invertebrates eat the small ones. Fish eat the invertebrates. Eagles, monitor lizards, humans and other apex consumers eat the fish.
AND BACK TO LANDThe link runs both waysDragonflies grow up in the water, then leave it as flying adults and become prey for birds. So some of the nutrients the hippos carried into the river travel back out again. Aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems are linked in both directions.
TAP A BUTTONOne animal, four effectsHippos are ecosystem engineers. Each button lights up one way they connect the grassland and the river.
HOW BIG IS THIS FLUX? Big. A hippo eats a great deal of grass every night and releases much of it into the water by day, and a river can hold thousands of hippos. Hippos alone supply a large share of the nitrogen and phosphorus that enter the river. One published estimate is that their dung and urine raise the river's nitrogen and phosphorus by roughly a quarter, about 25% (Subalusky and colleagues, 2015, as reported by Inside Science). It is a flux from the terrestrial pool to the freshwater pool, carried by an animal.
HOW DO YOU MEASURE THAT? Nobody can weigh what a wild hippo leaves in a river. So researchers measured hippos in a zoo pool: how much dung and urine they produce, and how much nitrogen and phosphorus is in it. A clean pool turned cloudy in less than a day. They then scaled those figures up to the number of hippos living along the river.
WHY THE SEASON MATTERS The same dung has opposite effects at different times. In the dry season the river is low and slow, so dung collects in the pools where hippos crowd together, and that is when oxygen can run out. When the rains return, the rising river flushes the pools out. That first rush can carry the oxygen-poor water downstream and kill fish there too, before the river recovers and the cycle starts again.
STEP 10 · WHEN THE CYCLE IS OVERLOADED

Dead zones

Humans now fix about as much nitrogen as nature does, and most of it goes onto fields. What is not taken up by crops runs off. Follow it downstream.

INTERACTIVE · SIX STEPS FROM FERTILIZER TO DEAD ZONE

Step through the chain of events

Tap Next step to go through all 6
FARMLANDO₂SEA FLOORNPNnutrients wash inALGAL BLOOMalgae die and sinkHUGE DETRITAL POOLdecomposers multiplyDEAD ZONEalmost no oxygen
1 OF 6 · NUTRIENTS ARRIVEInorganic nitrogen and phosphorus wash inRain carries excess fertilizer off farmland into streams and rivers. The Mississippi River delivers it to the Gulf of Mexico.
2 OF 6 · A BLOOMPhytoplankton grow explosivelyHere, nitrogen and phosphorus were the limiting nutrients: the ones in short supply. With the limit lifted, algae multiply into a "harmful" bloom. So far this is just eutrophication.
3 OF 6 · THE BLOOM DIESPhytoplankton diePhytoplankton are short-lived. A huge bloom means a huge number of dead cells, and they sink.
4 OF 6 · DEAD MATTER PILES UPA huge detrital poolAll that dead algae is detritus: a mountain of organic matter on the bottom, far more than usual.
5 OF 6 · DECOMPOSERS BOOMDecomposers increaseMore food for decomposers means more decomposers. Their population grows to match the detritus.
6 OF 6 · OXYGEN RUNS OUTOxygen declines: a dead zoneDecomposers carry out cellular respiration, which uses oxygen. So many of them use it faster than it is replaced. Oxygen in the water falls so low that fish and other animals leave or die.The process that removes the oxygen is cellular respiration by decomposers. Not the nutrients, and not the algae while they are alive.
THE CHAIN IN ONE LINE

Six links, in order

Nutrients inBloomAlgae dieDetritus piles upDecomposers increaseOxygen declines

A dead zone is the end of eutrophication: water with so little oxygen that most animals cannot live in it. The best-known one forms in the Gulf of Mexico, fed by runoff from the Mississippi River.

DATA · WHERE THE GULF'S NUTRIENTS COME FROM

Mostly from farming

NITROGEN
Corn and soybean crops · 52%Other crops · 14%Pasture and range · 5%Urban and population sources · 9%Atmospheric deposition · 16%Natural land · 4%
PHOSPHORUS
Corn and soybean crops · 25%Other crops · 18%Pasture and range · 37%Urban and population sources · 12%Natural land · 8%

Crops and pasture together supply about 71% of the nitrogen and 80% of the phosphorus. Excess nutrients are a problem in marine systems, not only in lakes.

SKETCH MAP · FROM FARM FIELDS TO THE GULF

One river system drains the country's farmland

most heavily farmedMississippi
RiverDEAD ZONE · Gulf of Mexicodashed line:
everything that
drains into ita sketch of the pattern, not measured values

Farmers apply nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizer. Crops take up only part of it. Rain washes the excess into streams, the streams join the Mississippi, and the Mississippi delivers it to the Gulf of Mexico. The dead zone forms there every summer and is at its largest in late summer.

TWO WORDS FOR TOO LITTLE OXYGEN

Hypoxia and anoxia

NORMALHYPOXIAANOXIAplenty of O₂under 2 mg
per liternone: 0
HYPOXIALow dissolved oxygen. Hypo means under. Scientists usually draw the line at less than 2 milligrams of oxygen per liter of water. Below that, most fish and bottom animals leave or die.
ANOXIANo dissolved oxygen at all. An means without. It is the extreme end of hypoxia.
A DEAD ZONEA stretch of hypoxic water. The Gulf of Mexico dead zone is mapped each summer by the 2 mg per liter line.
WHY IT GETS WORSE BY ITSELF

A loop that feeds itself

oxygen fallsanimals diemore detritusmore decomposingit feeds
itself

Phytoplankton (algae and cyanobacteria) live fast and die fast, so a bloom quickly turns into a huge detrital pool. As oxygen falls, more organisms die, which is more detritus, more decomposition, and even less oxygen.

INTERACTIVE · THE PATTERN THROUGH THE YEAR

Why the dead zone comes back every summer

Tap the buttons, or Next season, to click through all 3
O₂LANDSEA FLOORSPRINGrain washes fertilizer into the rivernutrients pour inSUMMERcalm, warm, layered waterriver water floats on topbottom layer: oxygen used upAUTUMNmixed againoxygen returns
SPRING · THE DELIVERYRain and snowmelt carry the fertilizer downstreamFields have just been fertilized, and spring rain and melting snow swell the rivers. The Mississippi delivers its biggest load of nitrogen and phosphorus of the year to the Gulf. Oxygen in the bottom water starts to fall.
SUMMER · THE DEAD ZONELayered water traps the problemThe sea is warm and calm. Lighter river water sits on top of the denser salty water, and the two layers barely mix. Algae bloom in the sunlit top layer, die, and sink. Decomposers in the bottom layer use up its oxygen, and no new oxygen can get down from the surface.The Gulf's bottom water is hypoxic for much of May to September, and the dead zone is at its largest in mid to late summer.
AUTUMN · THE RESETStorms and cold fronts stir it upTropical storms and the first cold fronts churn the water. The layers mix, oxygen from the surface reaches the bottom again, and the dead zone breaks up until the next year. It is a pattern that repeats every year, because the fertilizer arrives every spring.
THE YEARLY PATTERN

Three seasons, one cycle

1Spring
Rain carries fertilizer off the fields. The river's nutrient load peaks.
2Summer
Warm, calm, layered water. Bloom, die-off, decomposition. The bottom layer goes hypoxic.
3Autumn
Storms mix the layers. Oxygen returns, until next year.
Check yourself: the nutrients arrive in spring. Why is the dead zone worst in summer, not spring?

Two reasons. The chain takes time: bloom, then die-off, then decomposition. And in summer the water is layered and calm, so the bottom layer cannot be restocked with oxygen from the surface.

PUTTING THE MODULE TOGETHER

Why adding a nutrient can remove the oxygen

Every piece of this module is in that chain: a limiting nutrient is added, primary production jumps, the extra production becomes detritus, decomposers break it down, and their respiration uses up the oxygen.

Decomposition is essential, and usually invisible. A dead zone is what it looks like when there is suddenly far too much to decompose.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Eutrophication

Excessive growth of algae and aquatic plants after extra nutrients, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, reach the water.

Dead zone

A stretch of water with so little oxygen that most animals leave or die.

Lock it in · Part 3

  1. Nitrogen builds proteins and nucleic acids. Phosphorus builds ATP, nucleic acids and phospholipids.
  2. Producers take up ammonium, nitrate and phosphate and assimilate them. Heterotrophs get N and P from food.
  3. A pool (reservoir) is where an element is. A flux is the element moving. Detritus is a pool.
  4. The largest nitrogen pool is the atmosphere, and most producers cannot use it directly.
  5. Nitrogen fixation (N₂ → ammonia) is done only by some bacteria and archaea, such as Rhizobium in legume nodules. Denitrification sends nitrogen back to the air.
  6. Decomposition returns nitrogen and phosphorus from detritus to inorganic forms.
  7. Phosphate cycles quickly through organisms but very slowly through soil and ocean.
  8. Extra nutrients → bloom → algae die → detritus → decomposers → oxygen declines: a dead zone.
Vocab · 41 terms
Essential nutrient An element that is required for growth, reproduction or metabolic function.
Macronutrient A nutrient needed in large quantities. Macronutrients are the building blocks of proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates and phospholipids.
Limiting nutrient A nutrient that limits the growth of primary producers when it is in short supply. Nitrogen and phosphorus are limiting in some ecosystems.
Biogeochemical cycle The path an element takes as it moves from one pool to another within an ecosystem.
Pool A place where an element is held: the atmosphere, soil, water, or living things. Also called a reservoir or a compartment.
Reservoir Another word for a pool.
Flux The movement of an element from one pool to another.
Conservation of mass Matter is not created or destroyed. In an ecosystem, atoms are rearranged into new molecules and passed on, never used up.
Organic Carbon-containing molecules such as carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids. CO₂ is inorganic carbon.
Inorganic Not organic. Ammonium, nitrate, phosphate, CO₂ and N₂ gas are inorganic.
Detritus Dead matter and waste. Detritus is a pool, not a flux.
Detritivore An animal that eats detritus and breaks it into smaller pieces, such as an earthworm, a termite or a dung beetle.
Decomposers Bacteria, archaea, fungi and a few other eukaryotes that break complex organic molecules down into inorganic forms.
Decomposition The breakdown of detritus into inorganic forms that producers can use again.
Fungi Eukaryotes that are chemoheterotrophs. They digest food outside their bodies and absorb it, and their cell walls are made of chitin.
Chemoheterotroph An organism that gets both its energy and its carbon from organic molecules. Animals, fungi and many bacteria and archaea are chemoheterotrophs.
Chitin A complex carbohydrate (a polysaccharide that contains nitrogen) that makes fungal cell walls. Arthropod exoskeletons are made of it too. Strong but flexible, so the wall can hold turgor pressure.
Hyphae The thin threads that make up the body of a fungus. One thread is a hypha.
Mycelium The whole network of hyphae. The plural is mycelia.
Fruiting body The part of a fungus that produces and disperses spores. Mushrooms and puffballs are fruiting bodies.
Spores The tiny reproductive cells a fungus releases from its fruiting body. Each one can grow into a new mycelium.
Yeast A fungus that grows as single cells and does not form hyphae. Yeasts are used to make bread and beer.
Mycorrhizal fungi Fungi that grow in and around plant roots and act as an extension of them. They help the plant take up phosphate and get sugars in return.
Whale fall A dead whale that has sunk to the sea floor, and the community of scavengers, worms and bacteria that lives on it.
Ecosystem services Benefits that ecosystems provide, such as primary production. They depend on nutrients being recycled.
Assimilation Taking up an inorganic nutrient and building its atoms into organic molecules. Producers assimilate ammonium and nitrate.
Biosynthesis Building new organic molecules, such as proteins and nucleic acids.
Nitrogen fixation Turning N₂ gas into ammonia, a form living things can use. Only some bacteria and archaea can do it.
Rhizobium bacteria Nitrogen-fixing bacteria that live in nodules on the roots of legumes.
Eutrophication Excessive growth of algae and aquatic plants after extra nutrients, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, reach the water.
Dead zone A stretch of water with so little oxygen that most animals leave or die.
Extracellular digestion Digestion outside the cell. A fungus releases enzymes and the food is broken down in its surroundings.
Osmotrophy Feeding by absorbing dissolved molecules across the cell surface.
Turgor pressure The pressure that builds inside a walled cell as water flows in. In a hypha, it pushes the growing tip forward.
Ectomycorrhizae Mycorrhizae that form a sheath around the root tip, with threads between the root cells. They help the plant get nitrogen.
Endomycorrhizae Mycorrhizae that grow into the root cells and branch into arbuscules. The kind that matters most for phosphorus.
Nitrification The change of ammonium (NH₄⁺) to nitrite (NO₂⁻) and then nitrate (NO₃⁻), by nitrifying bacteria and archaea using oxygen.
Denitrification The change of nitrate (NO₃⁻) back to N₂ gas by microbes that respire with nitrate where there is no oxygen.
Ammonification The release of ammonia from dead matter by decomposers. It is the decomposition step of the nitrogen cycle.
Anammox Anaerobic ammonia oxidation: some bacteria and archaea combine ammonium with nitrite and release N₂ gas.
Weathering The slow chemical breakdown of rock. In the phosphorus cycle, it releases phosphate into soil and water.

Notes

Everything you are expected to know for this module, in the order the learning objectives ask for it. Read it once, then use the checklist at the end.

IN THESE NOTES1 · Biogeochemical cycles2 · Who the decomposers are3 · Fungi4 · What limits decomposition5 · Why decomposers matter6 · Phosphorus7 · The nitrogen cycle8 · Human impacts9 · Exam checklist
THE BIG IDEA

Energy passes through an ecosystem once, but atoms are reused. Decomposers (bacteria, archaea and fungi) turn the organic molecules in dead matter back into inorganic nutrients that producers can take up. Nitrogen and phosphorus cycle this way, and adding too much of them ends in a dead zone.

SECTION 1OBJECTIVE 1

How a biogeochemical cycle works

  • Energy flows, matter cycles. Energy leaves every food web as heat. The matter that cycles is atoms: carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and the rest.
  • A biogeochemical cycle is the path an element takes as it moves from one pool to another within an ecosystem. Bio: living things. Geo: air, soil, water, rock. Chemical: the element changes the molecule it is in.
  • Conservation of mass: atoms are not created or destroyed, only rearranged. That is why matter can cycle.
  • When something is eaten, its molecules are taken apart and rebuilt. A giraffe does not get the leaf's protein. It gets the leaf's amino acids and builds giraffe protein. Atoms are passed on, molecules are not.
ESSENTIAL NUTRIENTAn element required for growth, reproduction or metabolic function.
MACRONUTRIENTNeeded in large quantities. It does not mean a large molecule.
LIMITING NUTRIENTLimits the growth of primary producers when in short supply. Nitrogen and phosphorus are limiting in some ecosystems.

How nutrients enter and are altered: an inorganic nutrient is taken up by a producer and built into organic molecules, passed along by feeding, shed into detritus, and released as an inorganic nutrient again by decomposition.

SECTION 2OBJECTIVE 2

The major groups of decomposers, and where they sit on the tree of life

  • Bacteria, archaea and fungi, plus a few other eukaryotes. All three domains.
  • They are chemoheterotrophs: energy and carbon both come from organic molecules. Their food is detritus.
  • They move nutrients from the detrital pool back to the abiotic environment.
  • Decomposition starts with organic molecules and ends with inorganic ones: ammonium, nitrate (made from ammonium by other microbes) and phosphate.
WORDWHAT IT IS
DetritusDead matter and waste. A pool.
DetritivoreAn animal that eats detritus and breaks it into pieces: earthworm, termite, dung beetle.
DecomposerBacteria, archaea, fungi. They break organic molecules down chemically into inorganic forms.
DO NOT MIX THESE UPDetritivores shred. Decomposers convert. Smaller pieces have more surface for their volume, so shredding speeds up the decomposers' work.
SECTION 3OBJECTIVE 3

Fungi: domain, nutrition and cell walls

  • Domain Eukarya. Their closest relatives are animals, not plants.
  • All fungi are chemoheterotrophs. They release digestive enzymes, digest their food outside the body, and absorb the small molecules.
  • Cell walls of chitin, the same material as arthropod exoskeletons.
  • Most are multicellular. Yeasts are unicellular.
HYPHAEThe thin threads of the fungal body. One is a hypha.
MYCELIUMThe whole network of hyphae. Plural: mycelia.
FRUITING BODYThe part that makes and disperses spores. A mushroom, a puffball.
  • Much of a forest's biomass is underground, and about 50% of that is fungal tissue. Fungi are common, not rare.
  • An estimated 0.8 to 5.1 million species. Diversity is greatest at the equator and declines toward the poles, less sharply than plant diversity.
  • Strongest predictor of fungal species richness: mean annual precipitation. Soil properties such as pH also matter.
  • Two ecological roles: decomposers and mutualists. Mycorrhizal fungi help plants take up phosphate and get carbohydrates in return. About 85% of land plant species have them (also given as more than 90% of land plants).

How a fungus feeds

  • Two problems. Food such as cellulose is too big to absorb, so the fungus releases enzymes that cut it small. It cannot move, so it grows toward food as long thin hyphae.
  • Hyphae grow only at the tip, and the tip is where the enzymes are released. Growing forward is how a fungus both finds food and digests it.
  • On the menu: mostly dead plants. Cellulose is a chain of glucose and the most abundant biomolecule in and on soil. In wood it is bound up with lignin, which is even harder to break.
  • Bacteria also digest with released enzymes, but they barely move through soil. Hyphae grow out to find food, even into a tree trunk.
EXTRACELLULAR DIGESTIONDigestion outside the cell. The enzymes are released and the food is broken down out in the wood or soil.
OSMOTROPHYFeeding by absorbing dissolved molecules across the cell surface. The opposite of swallowing food.
TOGETHERDigest first, take in afterward. An animal does it the other way round.

Chitin, turgor and the push at the tip

  • Chitin is a complex carbohydrate: a modified polysaccharide that contains nitrogen. Arthropod exoskeletons are made of it too. It makes a wall that is strong but flexible.
  • Osmosis: a hypha holds more dissolved molecules than soil water, so water flows in.
  • The wall holds: a cell with no wall would burst. The chitin wall does not, so pressure builds up. This is turgor pressure.
  • The push: turgor pressure drives the growing tip forward through soil and into wood.
  • Changes in pressure along the hyphae also carry water and dissolved food through them, like sugar in a plant's phloem. That lets a fungus cross a patch with no food and build a mushroom above ground.

A body made of threads

  • Hyphae are 10 to 50 times thinner than a human hair. Long thin threads give a huge surface area for their volume, and a fungus feeds through its surface.
  • One mycelium of Armillaria ostoyae in Oregon covers more than 2,000 acres.
  • Picking every mushroom does not remove the fungus. The mycelium is still in the soil and wood, and it is by far the larger part.

Why rain matters so much

  • Eating happens in water: enzymes go out and food comes back dissolved, in a film of water around the hypha.
  • Growing needs water: turgor pressure is water flowing in.
  • Transport needs water: food moves through the hyphae in flowing water.
  • So a desert and a rainforest at the same latitude differ hugely in fungal species. Precipitation, not latitude alone, is the strongest predictor (Tedersoo et al. 2014, Nature).

Mycorrhizae: an extension of the root

ECTOMYCORRHIZAEA thick sheath of fungus around the root tip, with threads between the root cells. Gives the plant access to nitrogen.
ENDOMYCORRHIZAENothing shows outside. The fungus grows into root cells and branches into arbuscules. The kind that matters most for phosphorus.
  • Three reasons the threads beat the root: reach (the network stretches more than 10 cm past the root), thinness (they fit between soil particles), and enzymes (they make soil nutrients easier to take up).
  • A trade, not a gift. The plant pays its fungus 4% to 20% of all the carbohydrate it makes. In well-fertilized soil far fewer of its roots carry the fungus. In natural, nutrient-poor soils mycorrhizal roots are the norm.

Two potato experiments

  • 231 farm fields, North America and Europe, four years: 38.3 tons per hectare with no fungus added, 42.2 with it. That is 3.9 tons more, a gain of 9.5% (Hijri 2016, Mycorrhiza).
  • One field, two fertilizers: in year one, fungus added gave 33% more tubers with chemical fertilizer and 45% more with compost. In year two the gain was 10 to 20% (Douds et al. 2007).
  • The second field was already rich in phosphorus and the potatoes still did better, so the fungus helps in other ways too, such as making roots less open to infection.
  • The gain changed from year to year, and one potato variety did not respond at all.
READ THE BARS CAREFULLYThe gray bars are not plants with no fungus at all. Field soil already has some. The comparison is extra fungus added against none added.
SECTION 4OBJECTIVE 4

The abiotic factors that limit decomposition

FACTOREFFECT
TemperatureWarmer is faster, across the range measured.
MoistureModerate is fastest. Too dry: decomposers cannot work. Too wet: no oxygen.
OxygenMost decomposers respire with oxygen. Waterlogged places decompose slowly and dead matter piles up.
Quality of the detritusHigh quality (rich in nitrogen, low in lignin) is fast. Low quality (woody, high in lignin) is slow.
  • On the graph: the three separate lines show temperature, and the rise and fall along each line shows soil water. So the answer to "which variable" is both.
  • In aquatic environments, temperature is a key driver.
  • Whale falls: a carcass links biomes by carrying matter from the surface to the deep sea. Scavengers eat the flesh first, then snotworms and bacteria work on the bones. Whale populations were once 6 to 20 times higher, so there are fewer whale falls now.
SECTION 5OBJECTIVE 5

Decomposers, nutrient cycling and ecosystem services

  • Producers can only take up nutrients in inorganic form. Dead matter holds them in organic form.
  • Without decomposers, nutrients would stay locked in dead matter, producers would run out, and primary production would stop, along with every food web built on it.
  • The rate of decomposition limits how fast nutrients move through an ecosystem.
  • Decomposers recycle atoms. They do not recycle energy: they use it, and it leaves as heat.
SECTION 6OBJECTIVE 6

Phosphorus: form, uses, movement and eutrophication

  • Form producers use: phosphate. From soil on land, from the water column in water.
  • Why everything needs it: ATP, nucleic acids and phospholipids (cell membranes).
  • Up the food chain: by consumption. Heterotrophs get their P atoms from food.
  • Phosphate moves quickly through plants and animals, but very slowly through soil and ocean. There is no major gas pool.
  • Excess phosphorus in water drives eutrophication.

The whole cycle: eight arrows

STEPFROM → TOSPEED · WHO
1 · Weatheringphosphate in rock → PO₄³⁻ in soil and waterSlow. No organism.
2 · Uptake and assimilationPO₄³⁻ → ATP, nucleic acids, phospholipidsFast. Producers, helped by mycorrhizal fungi on land.
3 · Feedingproducer's molecules → consumer'sFast. Consumers.
4 · Decompositiondetritus → PO₄³⁻Fast. Decomposers.
5 · RunoffPO₄³⁻ in soil → rivers, lakes, the seaSlow. Water carries it. Fertilizer adds more.
6 · The fast loop, in waterPO₄³⁻ → phytoplankton → consumers → decomposersFast. Upwelling brings phosphate back up.
7 · Sedimentationphosphorus in the sea → sea-floor sedimentVery slow. No organism.
8 · Tectonic upliftsediment → rock in mountainsThe slowest step of all.
  • Most phosphorus is in rock. Producers use one form, the phosphate ion, PO₄³⁻.
  • Arrows 2, 3, 4 and 6 are the fast loops. Arrows 1, 5, 7 and 8 move phosphorus through soil, ocean and rock, and they slow the whole cycle.
THREE WAYS IT DIFFERS FROM NITROGENThe big pool is rock, not the atmosphere. There is one usable form, not two. And no step needs a microbe to change the form: phosphate is only passed along, taken up, eaten and released.
SECTION 7OBJECTIVE 7

The global nitrogen cycle

  • Largest pool: the atmosphere, as N₂ gas. Most producers cannot use it, because the triple bond is very hard to break.
  • Forms producers can take up: ammonium (NH₄⁺) and nitrate (NO₃⁻).
  • Why heterotrophs need N: proteins and nucleic acids. They get it from food.
  • Pool = reservoir = compartment: where the element is. Flux: the element moving. Detritus is a pool.
FLUXFROM → TOWHO
Nitrogen fixationN₂ → NH₃Some bacteria and archaea. Also lightning, and people.
Ammonia to ammoniumNH₃ → NH₄⁺No organism. Ammonia meets water.
NitrificationNH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻Nitrifying bacteria and archaea, using O₂. It is their energy source.
Uptake and assimilationNH₄⁺, NO₃⁻ → proteins, nucleic acidsPrimary producers
Feedingproducer → consumerConsumers
Decomposition (ammonification)detritus → NH₃Decomposers: bacteria, archaea, fungi
DenitrificationNO₃⁻ → N₂Denitrifying microbes, only where there is no O₂
AnammoxNH₄⁺ + NO₂⁻ → N₂ + 2 H₂OSome bacteria and archaea, in oxygen-poor water
N₂ + 8 H⁺ + 8 e⁻ → 2 NH₃ + H₂   (fixation)
NH₃ + H₂O → NH₄⁺ + OH⁻   (ammonia to ammonium)
NH₄⁺ + 2 O₂ → NO₃⁻ + H₂O + 2 H⁺   (nitrification)
  • Rhizobium: Bacteria. Mutualists in root nodules of legumes. They take N₂ from the atmospheric reservoir, fix it, and produce NH₄⁺. Not the only fixers: free-living microbes and Trichodesmium in the ocean do it too.
  • Tracing an atom: if feeding arrows alone cannot get you there, the atom must go through decomposition and back up from a producer. Name each process and say whether the molecule is organic or inorganic at each stop.
  • Nitrite (NO₂⁻) is the halfway form of nitrification.
  • Denitrification is anaerobic respiration. Most organisms hand their electrons to O₂ at the end of respiration. Denitrifiers use nitrate in its place. So it happens only where there is no oxygen: waterlogged soil, the mud under a lake, oxygen-poor water. Losing nitrogen to the air is a side effect of how the microbe gets its energy.
  • Anammox (anaerobic ammonia oxidation) is a second, smaller drain back to the air.
  • Why fixation can never stop: denitrification keeps sending usable nitrogen back to the air. If fixation stopped, usable nitrogen would slowly run down, and primary production with it.
  • Microbes run four of the six main fluxes: fixation, nitrification, decomposition, denitrification. Producers do uptake. Consumers do feeding.
THE THREE THINGS TO NEVER MIX UPProducers can take up only ammonium and nitrate. Fixation brings nitrogen in from the air and denitrification sends it back. Nitrification does neither: it only changes ammonium into nitrate.
SECTION 8OBJECTIVE 8

How humans have altered the nitrogen cycle, and eutrophication

  • Natural fixation: biological (far more common) and lightning.
  • Human sources of fixed nitrogen: industrial fertilizer, nitrogen-fixing crops, fossil fuels. Together they now add almost as much as all natural sources.
  • They all enter at the same arrow: nitrogen fixation.

The dead-zone chain, in order:

  • Excess inorganic N and P wash off farmland into rivers.
  • Phytoplankton bloom (eutrophication).
  • The phytoplankton die and sink.
  • A huge detrital pool forms.
  • Decomposers increase.
  • Their cellular respiration uses up the oxygen: oxygen declines, and the water becomes hypoxic (low oxygen) or anoxic (none).
THE STEP PEOPLE GET WRONGThe oxygen is used up by decomposers' respiration, not by the fertilizer and not by the living algae.
  • The Gulf of Mexico dead zone is fed by the Mississippi River, and its nutrients come mostly from farming. It forms every summer, when the water is warm, calm and layered.
  • Hippos carry N and P from land to river in their dung. A few hippos raise river NPP in the dry season. Too many use up the oxygen. On land their grazing makes grass stubbier and more nutritious.
SECTION 9

Exam checklist

You're ready when you can:

  • Explain "energy flows, matter cycles" and say what the matter is.
  • Say what happens to a protein when it is eaten.
  • Define macronutrient, limiting nutrient, pool, flux, assimilation.
  • Name the three groups of decomposers and place them in domains.
  • Tell a detritivore from a decomposer.
  • State whether decomposition starts and ends with organic or inorganic molecules.
  • Read the decomposition graph for both temperature and moisture, and explain the drop in wet soil.
  • Give four facts about fungi: domain, nutrition, cell wall, hyphae and mycelium.
  • Explain extracellular digestion and osmotrophy, and the two problems they solve.
  • Explain how osmosis, the chitin wall and turgor pressure push a hyphal tip forward.
  • Give three reasons rain matters so much to fungi.
  • Say what mycorrhizal fungi and plants exchange, what it costs the plant, and which kind (endo or ecto) matters most for phosphorus.
  • Read the two potato experiments and say what the gray bars mean.
  • Describe a whale fall and who lives there.
  • Name the molecules that contain N and the ones that contain P.
  • Draw the nitrogen cycle with six fluxes and say who does each. Add ammonium, nitrite and anammox for the full eight steps.
  • Explain why denitrification needs no oxygen, and why fixation can never stop.
  • List the eight arrows of the phosphorus cycle and say which are fast and which are slow.
  • Describe Rhizobium: domain, where it lives, what it does.
  • Trace a nitrogen atom between two organisms by the shortest path.
  • Say how hippos move nutrients and why the number of hippos matters.
  • Recite the dead-zone chain in order and name the process that removes the oxygen.

Infographics

Every diagram from the flow charts in one place, without the reading in between. Start with the one-page map, then scan the rest.

INFOGRAPHIC 1 · THE WHOLE MODULE ON ONE PAGE
MODULE 2.4 · PART 1

Matter cycles, and decomposition closes the loop

Every living thing eventually dies. What turns a dead leaf back into something a plant can use, and what decides how fast that happens?

1Energy flows. Matter cycles.
Module 2.3 ended with energy leaving every food web as heat. Matter is different. The atoms an organism is made of are never used up. They are passed on, taken apart, and built into something new.
2A giraffe eats a leaf. Where does the protein go?
The leaf contains protein. Does that same protein molecule end up in the giraffe? No. The molecule is taken apart. Its atoms are what move.
3Atoms are never used up: conservation of mass
Why can matter cycle at all? Because of one law. Matter is not created or destroyed. In living things and in ecosystems, atoms are only rearranged into new molecules and passed on.
4Decomposition: organic molecules in, inorganic nutrients out
Producers can only take up nutrients in simple inorganic forms. Everything that dies is made of complex organic molecules. Decomposition is the conversion of one back into the other.
5What controls the rate: temperature, water and oxygen
Decomposers are living things, so anything that speeds up or slows down their metabolism changes how fast nutrients are recycled.
6The quality of the detritus
Temperature, water and oxygen are about the conditions. The last control is about the dead matter itself. Not all detritus is equally easy to decompose.
7Detritivores: animals that break detritus into pieces
Before the chemistry there is often a mechanical step. Animals eat the detritus and break it into much smaller pieces. That does not finish the job, but it makes the job far faster.
MODULE 2.4 · PART 2

The decomposers: fungi and whale falls

Something has to do the work of decomposition. What kind of living thing is it, and why is most of it hidden?

1Who the decomposers are
Part 1 was about what decomposition does. This part is about who does it. One word describes how nearly all of them live, so learn it before you meet them.
2Fungi: the basics
Fungi are one of the major groups of decomposers, and on land they do most of the work. Four things to know about any fungus.
3Digest outside, then absorb
A fungus has no mouth and no gut. It feeds by absorbing molecules straight from its surroundings. That way of living creates two problems, and the whole body of a fungus is the answer to them.
4Chitin: why a fungus has a tough wall
Every fungal cell is wrapped in a wall of chitin. The wall is not there only for protection. It is what lets a thread as thin as a hair force its way through soil and into wood.
5The hidden forest
Ask someone to draw a fungus and they draw a mushroom. That is like drawing an apple and calling it the tree. Most of a fungus, and a surprising share of a whole forest, is underground.
6Fungal function and diversity
Fungi are one of the most diverse groups of eukaryotes, and they do two big jobs in an ecosystem.
7Mycorrhizae: an extension of the root
Not every fungus lives on dead matter. Mycorrhizal fungi grow in and around the roots of living plants. The name means "fungus-root".
8Whale falls: one carcass, a whole community
Everything so far has been on land. Decomposition happens in water too, with one main difference in what sets the speed.
MODULE 2.4 · PART 3

Nitrogen and phosphorus: following the atoms

Air is mostly nitrogen. So why is nitrogen so often the thing plants run short of, and what happens when we give them too much?

1What nitrogen and phosphorus are for
Parts 1 and 2 were about how nutrients get recycled, and who does it. This part follows two of the nutrients. Start with why every organism needs them.
2How N and P move through a food web
The same four moves carry nitrogen and phosphorus around every ecosystem. This is the giraffe and the leaf from Part 1, drawn as a loop.
3Pools and fluxes
Every biogeochemical cycle is described with two words. One is for where the element is . The other is for the element moving .
4The nitrogen cycle
Now put the pools and the fluxes together. Nitrogen starts in the air as N₂ gas, gets pulled into living things by microbes, moves through the food web, and is returned by microbes.
5Who fixes nitrogen, and how much
Nitrogen fixation is the only door from the huge atmospheric pool into the living world. Only prokaryotes can open it.
6Denitrification: usable nitrogen goes back to the air
Fixation is the door in. Denitrification is the door out. Where there is no oxygen, microbes turn nitrate back into N₂ gas, and that nitrogen is out of reach again.
7Trace one nitrogen atom
A standard exam task: follow a single atom from one organism to another, naming every process and the kind of molecule it is in at each stop. Try this one in an Antarctic food web.
8The phosphorus cycle
Phosphorus moves through pools just as nitrogen does, but it starts somewhere very different, and part of its journey is extremely slow.
9Hippos: a conveyor belt from land to water
Nutrients do not only cycle on the spot. Animals can carry them from one ecosystem into another. Hippos in the Mara River in Kenya are the classic case.
10Dead zones
Humans now fix about as much nitrogen as nature does, and most of it goes onto fields. What is not taken up by crops runs off. Follow it downstream.

BIOPart of the journey is inside living thingsNitrogen atoms sit inside organisms as part of their proteins and nucleic acids. They move along the food chain when one organism eats another.Example: a nitrogen atom in a leaf protein, then in a giraffe protein.

3 · Atoms are never used up: conservation of mass
INFOGRAPHIC 6
INTERACTIVE · FOLLOW ONE ATOM THROUGH TIME

Could an atom from a dinosaur be in you?

Tap the buttons, or Next stop, to click through all 5
ONE NITROGEN ATOM · MILLIONS OF YEARS →dinosaursoilplantanimalyouthe atom is in a protein in the dinosaurthe atom is in ammonium (NH₄⁺) in the soilthe atom is in a protein in a leafthe atom is in a protein in the animalthe atom is in a protein, or the DNA, of one of your cells
STOP 1 · LONG AGOA nitrogen atom is part of a dinosaurIt sits in a protein in the dinosaur's body. The dinosaur got it the way the giraffe did: from its food.
STOP 2 · THE DINOSAUR DIESDecomposers take the protein apartThe protein is broken down. The nitrogen atom is released into the soil as part of an inorganic molecule, ammonium. The atom is not destroyed. Only the molecule is.
STOP 3 · A PLANT TAKES IT UPBack into a living thingA plant's roots take up the ammonium, and the plant builds the nitrogen atom into one of its own proteins.
STOP 4 · AND AGAIN, AND AGAINAround the loop, over and overAn animal eats the plant. It dies, is decomposed, and the atom is taken up by another plant. This loop can repeat for millions of years, because nothing in it uses the atom up.
STOP 5 · TODAYThe same atom, in youYou eat. The atom is built into one of your proteins, or into your DNA. An atom that was once part of a dinosaur really can be part of you, because of the law of conservation of mass.This particular route is made up to show the idea. Nobody can follow a single atom. The principle is what is real.

CHEMO · WHERE THE ENERGY COMES FROMFrom chemicals, not from lightA chemotroph gets its energy by breaking chemical bonds in molecules. The opposite is photo: energy from sunlight.
HETERO · WHERE THE CARBON COMES FROMFrom other organismsHetero means "other". A heterotroph gets its carbon from organic molecules that some other organism made. The opposite is auto, "self": carbon taken straight from CO₂.

1 · ENZYMES OUT

The fungus releases digestive enzymes

Big molecules such as cellulose and starch cannot cross into a cell. So the hypha releases enzymes into whatever it is growing through. They are released at the growing tip.

2 · DIGESTION, OUTSIDE THE BODY

The enzymes break the food down

Out in the wood, the enzymes cut cellulose into single glucose molecules. This is extracellular digestion: digestion outside the cell.

3 · ABSORPTION

The small molecules are taken in

Glucose and other small molecules are absorbed straight across the wall and membrane. Feeding by absorbing dissolved molecules is called osmotrophy. A fungus digests first and takes the food in afterward.

4 · ON TO THE NEXT MEAL

It cannot walk, so it grows

A fungus has no way of moving. It finds food by growing. Where food is rich the hyphae grow fast and branch again and again. Where it is poor they slow down or stop.

4 · Chitin: why a fungus has a tough wall
INFOGRAPHIC 20
INTERACTIVE · ONE HYPHA IN SOIL

Water in, pressure up, tip forward

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
chitin wallwater flows in (osmosis)more dissolved
molecules insidethe chitin wall holds: no burstingTURGORpressure pushes the tip forwardsoil
1 · OSMOSIS

Water flows into the hypha

The inside of a hypha holds more dissolved molecules than the dilute water in soil. So water flows in by osmosis.

2 · THE WALL

Chitin stops it from bursting

A cell with no wall would swell and burst. The chitin wall holds, so the water coming in builds up pressure instead. It is called turgor pressure.

3 · THE PUSH

Pressure drives the tip forward

A hypha grows only at its tip. Turgor pressure provides the force that pushes the tip on, through soil and into wood. That is how a fungus finds its food.

INFOGRAPHIC 21
DIAGRAM · THE SAME PRESSURE MOVES FOOD

Food taken up here can be used over there

food heremushroomfood carried inside the hyphae

Changes in pressure along the hyphae push water and dissolved food through them, much like sugar moving through a plant's phloem. It lets a fungus grow across a patch with no food, and build a mushroom above the ground.

5 · The hidden forest
INFOGRAPHIC 22
INTERACTIVE · A FOREST, CUT AWAY

What is under the forest floor

Tap a button to explore
ABOVE GROUND · the small part you seeBELOW GROUNDMYCELIUM · all the hyphae togetherone hyphamushroomspuffballbracket fungi on
a living trunkspores
MYCELIUMThe body of the fungus is the networkAll the threads together are the mycelium (plural: mycelia). It runs through the soil, the leaf litter and the wood. This is the fungus. When you walk through a forest you are walking over an enormous amount of it.
ONE HYPHAA single threadOne thread is a hypha (plural: hyphae). Hyphae are 10 to 50 times thinner than a human hair. Being so long and thin gives them a huge surface for absorbing food.A hypha grows only at its tip, and it releases its digestive enzymes there. So growing forward is how a fungus both finds food and digests it.
FRUITING BODIESThe part you actually noticeA mushroom is a fruiting body. So is a white puffball, and so are the shelf-like brackets on a tree trunk. They are built by the mycelium for one job: making and releasing spores.Brackets on a standing tree are a sign that the fungus is already digesting its wood. Fungi do not wait for the tree to fall.
SPORESHow a fungus reproduces and spreadsSpores are tiny cells that rain out of the fruiting body and drift away on the air. One that lands on food can grow into a new mycelium. Spores are produced and dispersed during the fruiting-body stage of the life cycle.
TAP A BUTTON TO LIGHT UP ONE PARTThe mushroom is the tip of the icebergLook at how much of this picture is below the ground line. A mushroom is a small, short-lived part that a far bigger organism pushes up to release spores.

NEAR THE EQUATOR, WHERE IT IS WETThe most species of fungiFungal diversity is greatest at the equator. The warmest colors sit over tropical rainforest: the Amazon basin, Central America, South-East Asia.The reason shows up in the next button: these are the places with the most rain.

INFOGRAPHIC 25
DIAGRAM · CONNECTING THE DOTS

Why rain matters so much to a fungus

123water in the soil
1 · EATING HAPPENS IN WATERThe enzymes are released into the surroundings and the food comes back dissolved. Both need a film of water around the hypha.
2 · GROWING NEEDS WATERThe push at the tip is turgor pressure, and turgor pressure is water flowing in.
3 · TRANSPORT NEEDS WATERFood moves through the hyphae in flowing water.
SO THE PATTERN MAKES SENSE The strongest predictor of how many fungal species live in a place is mean annual precipitation. And decomposition speeds up where it is warm and moist. A body that eats, grows and moves food with water does best where there is water.

The map pattern is from Tedersoo et al. (2014), Nature. Soil properties such as pH matter too, so rain is the strongest factor, not the only one.

The threads reach where the root cannot

PLANT · makes sugarsFUNGAL HYPHAE ↓what the root
reaches alonephosphate → plantsugars → fungusP = phosphate

The hyphae are far thinner than any root, and there are far more of them. They work as an extension of the root system, scavenging nutrients from soil the root would never touch.

INFOGRAPHIC 27
INTERACTIVE · TWO KINDS OF MYCORRHIZAE

Which one helps with phosphorus?

Tap the buttons, or The other kind, to click through all 2
a sheath around the root tipthreads between the root cellsnothing to see from outsidearbuscules: inside the root cells
ECTOMYCORRHIZAE

A coat around the root

A thick sheath of fungal cells surrounds the root tip, and threads grow between the root cells. This kind gives the plant access to nitrogen it could not otherwise reach.

ENDOMYCORRHIZAE

Branched inside the root cells

Nothing shows on the outside. The fungus grows into the root cells and branches into tree-shaped arbuscules, a huge surface for trading. This is the kind that matters most for phosphorus.

Both kinds also send a wide network of threads out into the soil.

INFOGRAPHIC 28
NOT A GIFT · A TRADE THAT COSTS

Each partner is in it for itself

paid to the fungus: 4% to 20%kept by the plant

The plant pays for its fungus with 4% to 20% of all the carbohydrate it makes. That is a real cost.

poor soil: lots of fungusrich soil: very little

So the plant does not hand out sugar for nothing. Where the soil already supplies plenty of nutrients, as in a well-fertilized field, far fewer of its roots carry the fungus. In natural soils, nutrients are scarce, and mycorrhizal roots are the norm.

Neither side is being generous. The fungus takes sugars because it needs carbon. The plant gives them up because that is the price of phosphate.

INFOGRAPHIC 29
REAL EXPERIMENTS · POTATOES, WITH AND WITHOUT ADDED FUNGUS

What the fungus is worth to the plant

no fungus added mycorrhizal fungus added
EXPERIMENT 1 · 231 FARM FIELDS
38.342.2no fungus addedfungus addedtons of potatoes per hectare

One mycorrhizal fungus was added to seed potatoes in 231 field trials across North America and Europe over four years. Fields with the fungus averaged 3.9 tons more per hectare, a gain of 9.5%.

Hijri (2016), Mycorrhiza 26: 209 to 214.

EXPERIMENT 2 · ONE FIELD, TWO KINDS OF FERTILIZER
100133100145chemical fertilizercomposttuber yield · no fungus added = 100

Potato plots were given mycorrhizal fungi or none. In the first year the plots with fungi yielded 33% more with chemical fertilizer and 45% more with compost. In the second year the gain was smaller, 10 to 20%.

Douds, Nagahashi, Reider and Hepperly (2007), Biological Agriculture and Horticulture 25: 67 to 78.

READ THE BARS CAREFULLYThe gray bars are not plants with no fungus at all. Field soil already has some. The comparison is extra fungus added against none added.
IT IS NOT ONLY PHOSPHATEThe second field was already very rich in phosphorus, and the potatoes still did better. Mycorrhizae can help in other ways too, such as making roots less open to infection.
IT DOES NOT ALWAYS WORKThe size of the gain changed from year to year, and in the same group's trials one potato variety did not respond at all.
8 · Whale falls: one carcass, a whole community
INFOGRAPHIC 30
INTERACTIVE · WHAT HAPPENS TO A DEAD WHALE

A whale fall, stage by stage

Tap the buttons, or Next stage, to click through all 4
sunlit surface · where the whale feddeep sea · cold, dark, little fooda whale dies
and sinksSTAGE 1 · the fleshhagfishsharkcrabsSTAGE 2 · the bonesSNOTWORMS
growing on the bonesBACTERIA
purple matsAFTERWARDS · open questionswhere do the young
snotworms go next?
THE FALLA whale dies near the surface and sinksThe whale spent its life feeding in the sunlit upper ocean. When it dies, all of that organic matter sinks to the sea floor, where food is scarce. The carcass links two biomes: matter made near the surface now feeds the deep.
STAGE 1 · SCAVENGERSFlesh-eating animals arrive firstOnce the carcass is on the bottom, mobile scavengers find it and eat the soft tissue: hagfish, sharks, crabs and other arthropods. They strip the flesh down to the skeleton.
STAGE 2 · THE SKELETONThen the bones are eaten tooWith the flesh gone, a different community takes over. Bacteria feed on what is left in and around the bones. Snotworms, bone-eating worms, grow on the skeleton itself.It is cold down here, and temperature is a key driver of decomposition in water, so this stage is slow.
AFTERWARDSA lot is still unknownA whale fall is a rare island of food in a huge, empty sea floor. Snotworms need bones to live on. So when one skeleton is used up, where do they go, and how do their young find the next one? Nobody is sure yet. Much about these communities is still being worked out.

Whale populations were once 6 to 20 times higher than they are now. Hunting removed most of them.

INFOGRAPHIC 33
INTERACTIVE · FIVE MOLECULES, WITH N AND P MARKED

See where the nitrogen and the phosphorus actually sit

Tap the buttons, or Next molecule, to click through all 5

groupsPHOSPHOLIPID · phospho + lipidphosphate

lipid parta cell membrane: two layers of themCARBOHYDRATE · a sugarcarbon, hydrogen and oxygen only: no N, no P
PROTEIN · NEEDS NITROGENNitrogen in every amino acidA protein is a chain of amino acids. Each amino acid begins with a nitrogen atom, so a protein is full of nitrogen. No phosphorus in the chain itself.
NUCLEIC ACIDS · NEED BOTHPhosphorus in the backbone, nitrogen in the basesDNA and RNA are chains of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has a phosphate group (phosphorus), a sugar, and a base (the bases are rings that contain nitrogen). So nucleic acids need both N and P.
ATP · NEEDS BOTHThree phosphates on a nucleotideATP is a nucleotide with three phosphate groups in a row. That is where the name comes from: adenosine triphosphate. Its base, adenine, contains nitrogen. Every cell makes and spends ATP constantly.
PHOSPHOLIPID · NEEDS PHOSPHORUSThe main use of phosphorus in a cellRead the word in two halves: phospho + lipid. A phosphate head on two fatty tails. It belongs to the class of molecules called lipids, or fats. Every cell membrane is a double layer of phospholipids, so every cell needs a great deal of them.
CARBOHYDRATE · NEEDS NEITHERJust carbon, hydrogen and oxygenSugars, starch and cellulose contain no nitrogen and no phosphorus. That is why a producer can make sugar from CO₂ and water alone, but cannot grow without taking up N and P as well.

INFOGRAPHIC 35
INTERACTIVE · FOLLOW AN ATOM AROUND THE LOOP

Consumption carries N and P up. Decomposition brings them back.

Tap Next move to go through all 5
NH₄⁺ NO₃⁻ PO₄³⁻SOILPRODUCERHERBIVOREPREDATORDETRITUSDECOMPOSERSuptake +
assimilationherbivorypredationdeath

1 · UPTAKE AND ASSIMILATIONInorganic in the soil → organic in a producerUptake: the roots take in ammonium, nitrate and phosphate ions. Assimilation: the plant builds those atoms into its own organic molecules: proteins, nucleic acids, ATP, phospholipids. This is the only place where N and P go from inorganic to organic.
2 · CONSUMPTION: HERBIVORYA consumer eats a producerConsumption is eating. When the food is a producer it is called herbivory. Then digestion: the giraffe breaks the plant's big molecules into small ones (proteins into amino acids). Then biosynthesis: it builds its own molecules from them.
3 · CONSUMPTION: PREDATIONA consumer eats a consumerWhen the food is another animal, consumption is called predation. The steps inside are the same: digest the prey's molecules, rebuild them as your own. N and P move up the food chain by consumption, one level at a time, always inside organic molecules.
4 · DEATH AND WASTEEverything ends up as detritusWhatever dies without being eaten, and everything that is excreted, joins the detritus. The nitrogen and phosphorus are still locked in organic molecules, which producers cannot take up.
5 · DECOMPOSITIONOrganic → inorganic, and the loop closesDecomposers break the organic molecules down and release the atoms in inorganic form: ammonium (some of which other microbes turn into nitrate) and phosphate. Those are available to primary producers again. Back to step 1.

THE POOLSWhere the nitrogen isEach box is a pool with the amount it holds. The atmosphere dwarfs everything else. Vegetation and marine life, the living pools, are tiny by comparison. You do not need to memorize the numbers, only which is biggest.
FLUX · NATURAL NITROGEN FIXATIONOut of the air, by microbesBacteria and archaea on land and in the ocean pull N₂ out of the atmosphere and turn it into forms living things can use. This is the main natural way nitrogen enters ecosystems.
FLUX · HUMAN NITROGEN FIXATIONOut of the air, by usFactories fix nitrogen to make fertilizer, and farmers plant crops such as soybeans whose root bacteria fix nitrogen. Compare the numbers with the last step: human fixation is now about as large as natural fixation on land.
FLUX · DENITRIFICATIONBack into the airOther microbes turn nitrate back into N₂ gas, which returns to the atmosphere. Rivers also carry nitrogen from the land pool to the ocean pool: that is a flux too.

Numbers are from the published global figure. They are there to compare sizes, not to memorize.

INFOGRAPHIC 41
INTERACTIVE · THE CHEMISTRY, ONE REACTION AT A TIME

Why N₂ is so hard to use, and how microbes manage it

Tap the buttons, or Next reaction, to click through all 5
N₂ · NITROGEN GASthree bonds between the two atomsvery stable · very hard to breakNITROGEN FIXATION+ 8 Hinside a nitrogen-fixing bacterium2 NH₃ · ammoniaN₂ + 8 H⁺ + 8 e⁻ → 2 NH₃ + H₂costs the cell a lot of ATPAMMONIA → AMMONIUMNH₃
ammoniaNH₄⁺
ammonium+ waterNH₃ + H₂O → NH₄⁺ + OH⁻NITRIFICATIONNH₄⁺NO₂⁻
nitriteNO₃⁻
nitratehydrogens off, oxygens on · uses O₂DENITRIFICATION2 NO₃⁻ · nitrateN₂ gasoxygens off · happens where there is no O₂
THE PROBLEM · A TRIPLE BONDWhy the biggest pool is out of reachIn N₂ gas the two nitrogen atoms share three bonds. A triple bond is extremely stable, so it takes a great deal of energy to pull the atoms apart. Plants, animals and fungi have no way of doing it. That is why air that is 78% nitrogen cannot feed a plant.
NITROGEN FIXATIONBreak the bond, add hydrogensNitrogen-fixing bacteria and archaea have an enzyme, nitrogenase, that can break the triple bond. As the atoms come apart, hydrogens are added to each one, giving two molecules of ammonia, NH₃.Where the hydrogen comes from: hydrogen ions (H⁺) that are always present in the watery inside of the cell, plus electrons (e⁻) that the bacterium takes from its food. An H⁺ and an electron together make one hydrogen atom. The reaction is costly: the cell spends a lot of ATP on it.
AMMONIA BECOMES AMMONIUMOne more hydrogen, from waterAmmonia dissolves in the water in soil, lakes and the sea, and picks up a hydrogen ion from the water. It is now ammonium, NH₄⁺. So NH₃ and NH₄⁺ are the same nitrogen, one hydrogen apart, and in wet places you mostly find ammonium.
NITRIFICATIONAmmonium is switched to nitrateNitrifying bacteria and archaea take the hydrogens off the nitrogen and put oxygens on instead: first nitrite (NO₂⁻), then nitrate (NO₃⁻). They do it to get energy, and they use oxygen gas to do it. Overall: NH₄⁺ + 2 O₂ → NO₃⁻ + H₂O + 2 H⁺.
DENITRIFICATIONThe reverse trip, back to N₂Where there is no oxygen gas, such as waterlogged soil, some bacteria use the oxygen in nitrate for their respiration instead. The oxygens are stripped off, the nitrogen atoms pair up again, and N₂ gas escapes to the air. Usable nitrogen has been lost from the soil.

Where each flux happens: in the air, in the soil, in the water

NITROGEN FIXATION · N₂ → NH₃Four routes down from the airRhizobium in the root nodules of legumes. Free-living bacteria and archaea in the soil. Trichodesmium, a cyanobacterium, in the ocean. And lightning, the one route that is not biological. All of them turn N₂ gas into a form that ends up in soil or water.
NITRIFICATION · NH₃ → NO₃⁻In the soil and in waterNitrifying microbes turn ammonia into nitrate. It happens wherever there is ammonia and oxygen, on land and in water, which is why nitrate is the most common usable form in both.
UPTAKE AND ASSIMILATIONTwo forms, two kinds of producerOn land, plant roots take up ammonium and nitrate from the soil. In water, phytoplankton take the same two ions straight from the water around them. No roots are needed: the nutrients come in across the surface of each cell.Either way, the producer then assimilates the nitrogen: it builds it into amino acids, proteins and nucleic acids.
DECOMPOSITION · ORGANIC N → NH₃At the surface and in the soilDead leaves, dead animals and dung are broken down by decomposers, which return the nitrogen to the soil as ammonia. In water, dead cells sink and are decomposed on the way down and on the bottom.
DENITRIFICATION · NO₃⁻ → N₂The reverse of fixation, in airless placesIn waterlogged soil and other places with no oxygen, denitrifying bacteria use nitrate in their respiration and release N₂ gas. This is the arrow that returns nitrogen to the atmosphere and closes the whole cycle.

6 · Denitrification: usable nitrogen goes back to the air
INFOGRAPHIC 47
INTERACTIVE · SAME SOIL, TWO CONDITIONS

Take the oxygen away and watch the nitrate

Tap the buttons, or Flood the soil, to click through all 2
NO₃⁻microbeO₂ in the
soil poresnitrate stays
for the rootsflooded:
no O₂N₂ gas escapesnitrate leaves
as N₂
WITH OXYGEN

Nothing is lost

The spaces between soil grains hold air. Microbes respire with oxygen, as most organisms do. Nitrate stays in the soil, and roots take it up.

NO OXYGEN

Nitrate is used in place of oxygen

Water has filled the spaces, and the oxygen is used up. Denitrifying microbes switch to nitrate for their respiration. The nitrogen comes out as N₂ gas and bubbles away. The soil now holds less usable nitrogen.

INFOGRAPHIC 48
DIAGRAM · WHY A MICROBE WOULD DO THIS

It is how they respire without oxygen

MOST ORGANISMSDENITRIFIERSO₂H₂ONO₃⁻N₂respirationrespiration

Respiration needs something to hand electrons to at the end. Most organisms use oxygen. Denitrifiers use nitrate in its place. This is anaerobic respiration.

So the microbe is not trying to remove nitrogen. Losing it to the air is a side effect of how the microbe gets its energy.

INFOGRAPHIC 49
DIAGRAM · IN AND OUT

Why fixation can never stop

AIR · N₂ gasNH₄⁺ and NO₃⁻usable nitrogen in soil and waterfixation
INdenitrification
OUT

Denitrification is very good at sending nitrogen back to the air. If fixation stopped, the usable nitrogen would slowly run down, and primary production would run down with it.

Anammox is a second, smaller drain: some microbes in oxygen-poor water combine ammonium with nitrite and release N₂.

Whale protein.Why this is the shortest path: nothing eats an elephant seal and is then eaten by a baleen whale, so the atom has to go down through the decomposers and back up through the producers.

ONE NITROGEN ATOMAir → soil → plant → animal → detritus → soil → airFixation brings it out of the air. A plant takes it up and assimilates it into protein. An animal gets it by consumption, digests the protein, and rebuilds its own. After death, decomposition releases it as ammonium. From there it is either taken up again, which is the short loop most atoms follow many times, or denitrified back to the air.
ONE PHOSPHORUS ATOMRock → soil → plant → animal → detritus → soilThere is no gas stop. Weathering slowly releases phosphate from rock into soil. A plant takes it up and assimilates it into DNA, ATP and phospholipids. Consumption and digestion pass it up the food chain. Decomposition returns it as phosphate, and the fast loop repeats. Some washes to the sea, sinks into sediment, and takes an enormously long time to become rock on land again.
ONE CARBON ATOMAir → plant → animal → detritus → decomposer → airPhotosynthesis takes it from CO₂ into a sugar. The plant builds the sugar into other molecules. An animal eats and digests them. At every stop, cellular respiration can send the atom straight back to the air as CO₂, and decomposers send back whatever is left. Module 2.5 follows carbon in full.
8 · The phosphorus cycle
INFOGRAPHIC 52
EVERY STEP · THE WHOLE PHOSPHORUS CYCLE ON ONE CARD

Rock to rock: eight arrows, one usable form, and no gas

Phosphorus is simpler than nitrogen. Most of it is in rock, not in the air. Producers use one form, the phosphate ion, PO₄³⁻. No microbe has to change it into another form first.

ROCKPO₄³⁻ in soilSEASEDIMENT12345678
1Weathering
phosphate locked in rock→PO₄³⁻ in soil and water
PHOSPHORUS ENTERS THE FOOD WEBWho: no organism. Rock breaks down chemically.Speed: slow.
2Uptake and assimilation
PO₄³⁻ in soil, or in the water column→ATP, nucleic acids, phospholipids
INORGANIC → ORGANICWho: primary producers. On land, mycorrhizal fungi help. In water, it comes from the water column.Speed: fast.
3Feeding
producer's molecules→consumer's molecules
Who: consumers. Their P atoms come from food.Speed: fast.
4Decomposition
detritus→PO₄³⁻
ORGANIC → INORGANICWho: decomposers. Some phosphate is taken straight back up. Some is carried away by water.Speed: fast.
5Runoff
PO₄³⁻ in soil→rivers, lakes, the sea
Who: no organism. Water carries it. Fertilizer washed off fields adds more and drives eutrophication.Speed: slow.
6The same fast loop, in the water
PO₄³⁻ in the water column→producers→consumers→decomposers
Who: phytoplankton, their consumers, and decomposers, in sunlit water. Upwelling can bring phosphate back up from deep water.Speed: fast.
7Sedimentation
phosphorus in the sea→sediment on the sea floor
PHOSPHORUS LEAVES THE FOOD WEBWho: no organism. What sinks builds up on the sea floor.Speed: very slow.
8Tectonic uplift
sediment→rock in mountains
Who: no organism. Sediments are raised into mountains, and weathering can start again.Speed: the slowest step of all.
FAST INSIDE, SLOW OUTSIDE Arrows 2, 3, 4 and 6 are the fast loops: phosphate moves quickly through plants and animals. Arrows 1, 5, 7 and 8 move phosphorus through soil, ocean and rock, and they are very slow. That is what slows the whole cycle.
THREE WAYS IT DIFFERS FROM NITROGEN The big pool is rock, not the atmosphere. There is one usable form, not two. And no step needs a microbe to change the form: phosphate is only passed along, taken up, eaten and released.

Hippos graze on grassland at night and spend the day in the water, where they release dung and urine. Every day they move carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus from the terrestrial system into the freshwater one. Rainfall, runoff and gravity usually do this job. Here an animal does.

INFOGRAPHIC 55
INTERACTIVE · THE SAME POOL, FEW HIPPOS OR MANY

When fertilizer becomes too much

Tap the buttons, or Add more hippos, to click through all 2
O₂A FEW HIPPOSa little dung = fertilizermore algae · NPP goes UPMANY HIPPOSfar too much dungdecomposers use up the O₂fish die · NPP goes DOWN
DRY SEASON · A FEW HIPPOSA helpful dose of fertilizerThe dung and urine bring nitrogen and phosphorus that the river's producers were short of. Algae grow faster, so net primary productivity goes up, and there is more food for the whole aquatic food web.
DRY SEASON · MANY HIPPOSToo much of a good thingIn the dry season the river is low and slow, so dung piles up instead of washing away. It is a huge load of detritus. Decomposers multiply to break it down, and their respiration uses up the oxygen in the water. Fish die, the water turns murky, and productivity falls.This is the idea to hold on to for the rest of the module: a burst of decomposition strips oxygen out of water.

ON LAND · HIPPO LAWNSGrazing changes the grassWhere hippos graze night after night, the grass is kept closely cropped. It grows back stubbier and leafier, which makes it more nutritious. Other herbivores benefit from these lawns.
IN THE WATER · DUNGFertilizer, and foodDung is a fertilizer for algae and microbes, and it is food for scavenger fish. Nitrogen and phosphorus that were in grass on land are now in the river: a flux from the terrestrial system to the freshwater one.
UP THE AQUATIC FOOD WEBThe nutrients keep movingMicroorganisms are food for aquatic invertebrates. Predatory invertebrates eat the small ones. Fish eat the invertebrates. Eagles, monitor lizards, humans and other apex consumers eat the fish.
AND BACK TO LANDThe link runs both waysDragonflies grow up in the water, then leave it as flying adults and become prey for birds. So some of the nutrients the hippos carried into the river travel back out again. Aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems are linked in both directions.

10 · Dead zones
INFOGRAPHIC 57
INTERACTIVE · SIX STEPS FROM FERTILIZER TO DEAD ZONE

Step through the chain of events

Tap Next step to go through all 6
FARMLANDO₂SEA FLOORNPNnutrients wash inALGAL BLOOMalgae die and sinkHUGE DETRITAL POOLdecomposers multiplyDEAD ZONEalmost no oxygen
1 OF 6 · NUTRIENTS ARRIVEInorganic nitrogen and phosphorus wash inRain carries excess fertilizer off farmland into streams and rivers. The Mississippi River delivers it to the Gulf of Mexico.
2 OF 6 · A BLOOMPhytoplankton grow explosivelyHere, nitrogen and phosphorus were the limiting nutrients: the ones in short supply. With the limit lifted, algae multiply into a "harmful" bloom. So far this is just eutrophication.
3 OF 6 · THE BLOOM DIESPhytoplankton diePhytoplankton are short-lived. A huge bloom means a huge number of dead cells, and they sink.
4 OF 6 · DEAD MATTER PILES UPA huge detrital poolAll that dead algae is detritus: a mountain of organic matter on the bottom, far more than usual.
5 OF 6 · DECOMPOSERS BOOMDecomposers increaseMore food for decomposers means more decomposers. Their population grows to match the detritus.
6 OF 6 · OXYGEN RUNS OUTOxygen declines: a dead zoneDecomposers carry out cellular respiration, which uses oxygen. So many of them use it faster than it is replaced. Oxygen in the water falls so low that fish and other animals leave or die.The process that removes the oxygen is cellular respiration by decomposers. Not the nutrients, and not the algae while they are alive.

RiverDEAD ZONE · Gulf of Mexicodashed line:

Farmers apply nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizer. Crops take up only part of it. Rain washes the excess into streams, the streams join the Mississippi, and the Mississippi delivers it to the Gulf of Mexico. The dead zone forms there every summer and is at its largest in late summer.

INFOGRAPHIC 60
TWO WORDS FOR TOO LITTLE OXYGEN

Hypoxia and anoxia

NORMALHYPOXIAANOXIAplenty of O₂under 2 mg
per liternone: 0
HYPOXIALow dissolved oxygen. Hypo means under. Scientists usually draw the line at less than 2 milligrams of oxygen per liter of water. Below that, most fish and bottom animals leave or die.
ANOXIANo dissolved oxygen at all. An means without. It is the extreme end of hypoxia.
A DEAD ZONEA stretch of hypoxic water. The Gulf of Mexico dead zone is mapped each summer by the 2 mg per liter line.
INFOGRAPHIC 61
WHY IT GETS WORSE BY ITSELF

A loop that feeds itself

oxygen fallsanimals diemore detritusmore decomposingit feeds
itself

Phytoplankton (algae and cyanobacteria) live fast and die fast, so a bloom quickly turns into a huge detrital pool. As oxygen falls, more organisms die, which is more detritus, more decomposition, and even less oxygen.

INFOGRAPHIC 62
INTERACTIVE · THE PATTERN THROUGH THE YEAR

Why the dead zone comes back every summer

Tap the buttons, or Next season, to click through all 3
O₂LANDSEA FLOORSPRINGrain washes fertilizer into the rivernutrients pour inSUMMERcalm, warm, layered waterriver water floats on topbottom layer: oxygen used upAUTUMNmixed againoxygen returns
SPRING · THE DELIVERYRain and snowmelt carry the fertilizer downstreamFields have just been fertilized, and spring rain and melting snow swell the rivers. The Mississippi delivers its biggest load of nitrogen and phosphorus of the year to the Gulf. Oxygen in the bottom water starts to fall.
SUMMER · THE DEAD ZONELayered water traps the problemThe sea is warm and calm. Lighter river water sits on top of the denser salty water, and the two layers barely mix. Algae bloom in the sunlit top layer, die, and sink. Decomposers in the bottom layer use up its oxygen, and no new oxygen can get down from the surface.The Gulf's bottom water is hypoxic for much of May to September, and the dead zone is at its largest in mid to late summer.
AUTUMN · THE RESETStorms and cold fronts stir it upTropical storms and the first cold fronts churn the water. The layers mix, oxygen from the surface reaches the bottom again, and the dead zone breaks up until the next year. It is a pattern that repeats every year, because the fertilizer arrives every spring.
