Decomposition & Nutrient Cycles

How dead matter is turned back into nutrients, who does the work, and how nitrogen and phosphorus travel around an ecosystem.

02 / 33 · MODULE 2.4 · PART 1 · THE QUESTION

Matter cycles, and decomposition closes the loop

Every living thing eventually dies. What turns a dead leaf back into something a plant can use, and what decides how fast that happens?

03 / 33 · PART 1 · 1 OF 7

Energy flows. Matter cycles.

Module 2.3 ended with energy leaving every food web as heat. Matter is different. The atoms an organism is made of are never used up. They are passed on, taken apart, and built into something new.

DIAGRAM · A LINE AND A LOOP

Two different journeys

ENERGY
passes through onceMATTER · goes aroundProducersConsumersheatsunProducersConsumersDetritusNutrients

"Matter" means atoms: carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and the other elements living things are built from. They cycle between organisms and the abiotic environment: the soil, the water and the air.

04 / 33 · PART 1 · 2 OF 7

A giraffe eats a leaf. Where does the protein go?

The leaf contains protein. Does that same protein molecule end up in the giraffe? No. The molecule is taken apart. Its atoms are what move.

DIAGRAM · ONE PROTEIN, FOLLOWED THROUGH A MEAL

Same beads, different chain

PROTEIN
IN THE LEAFAMINO
ACIDSPROTEIN IN
THE GIRAFFEdigestion
chain taken apartbiosynthesis
a new chain built

Each bead is an amino acid, and each one carries nitrogen (N). The giraffe ends up with the leaf's nitrogen atoms, built into giraffe proteins. It is not the same protein that was in the leaf.

05 / 33 · PART 1 · 3 OF 7

Atoms are never used up: conservation of mass

Why can matter cycle at all? Because of one law. Matter is not created or destroyed. In living things and in ecosystems, atoms are only rearranged into new molecules and passed on.

INTERACTIVE · FOLLOW ONE ATOM THROUGH TIME

Could an atom from a dinosaur be in you?

Tap the buttons, or Next stop, to click through all 5
ONE NITROGEN ATOM · MILLIONS OF YEARS →dinosaursoilplantanimalyouthe atom is in a protein in the dinosaurthe atom is in ammonium (NH₄⁺) in the soilthe atom is in a protein in a leafthe atom is in a protein in the animalthe atom is in a protein, or the DNA, of one of your cells
STOP 1 · LONG AGOA nitrogen atom is part of a dinosaurIt sits in a protein in the dinosaur's body. The dinosaur got it the way the giraffe did: from its food.
STOP 2 · THE DINOSAUR DIESDecomposers take the protein apartThe protein is broken down. The nitrogen atom is released into the soil as part of an inorganic molecule, ammonium. The atom is not destroyed. Only the molecule is.
STOP 3 · A PLANT TAKES IT UPBack into a living thingA plant's roots take up the ammonium, and the plant builds the nitrogen atom into one of its own proteins.
STOP 4 · AND AGAIN, AND AGAINAround the loop, over and overAn animal eats the plant. It dies, is decomposed, and the atom is taken up by another plant. This loop can repeat for millions of years, because nothing in it uses the atom up.
STOP 5 · TODAYThe same atom, in youYou eat. The atom is built into one of your proteins, or into your DNA. An atom that was once part of a dinosaur really can be part of you, because of the law of conservation of mass.This particular route is made up to show the idea. Nobody can follow a single atom. The principle is what is real.
06 / 33 · PART 1 · 4 OF 7

Decomposition: organic molecules in, inorganic nutrients out

Producers can only take up nutrients in simple inorganic forms. Everything that dies is made of complex organic molecules. Decomposition is the conversion of one back into the other. Hold on to this one sentence before meeting any decomposer by name.

DIAGRAM · THE ONE THING DECOMPOSITION DOES

in soil and waterDECOMPOSERSproteins, DNA, RNA
big and complexNH₄⁺NO₃⁻PO₄³⁻small and simple:
producers can
take these up

Decomposition starts with organic molecules and ends with inorganic ones. Those inorganic forms are exactly the ones producers can use.

Decomposers are living things, so anything that speeds up or slows down their metabolism changes how fast nutrients are recycled.

The quality of the detritus

Temperature, water and oxygen are about the conditions. The last control is about the dead matter itself. Not all detritus is equally easy to decompose.

INTERACTIVE · THREE KINDS OF DEAD MATTER

Why a leaf rots faster than a log

Tap a button to explore
SOFT TISSUE
loose moleculesCELLULOSE
tightly packedWOOD
plus ligninbreaks down
FASTbreaks down
more slowlybreaks down
SLOWESTpink shapes = decomposers' enzymes
HIGH QUALITYEasy to get into, and rewardingSoft tissue that is rich in nutrients, such as a fresh green leaf, fruit, or animal remains. Enzymes can reach the molecules easily, so it disappears quickly.
LOWER QUALITYCellulose: a complex carbohydrateCellulose is the main material of plant cell walls. It is a long chain of glucose, so it is rich in carbon and energy. But the chains bind tightly to one another, which makes it hard to break down. Tough leaves and stems take longer.
LOWEST QUALITYWood: cellulose locked inside ligninIn wood, the cellulose is wrapped in lignin, a tough material with no regular structure for an enzyme to grip. A few bacteria can break lignin down, but in nature fungi do most of the decomposition of wood, and they need oxygen to do it.That is why a log can lie on a forest floor for years after the leaves around it are long gone.
TAP A KIND OF DETRITUSZoom in to the molecules"Quality" is how easy the detritus is for decomposers to break down. Tap each box to see why one kind goes faster than another.
09 / 33 · PART 1 · 7 OF 7

Detritivores: animals that break detritus into pieces

Before the chemistry there is often a mechanical step. Animals eat the detritus and break it into much smaller pieces. That does not finish the job, but it makes the job far faster.

INTERACTIVE · WHY SMALLER PIECES ROT FASTER

Surface area for the same volume

Tap the buttons, or Shred it, to click through all 2
1 piece · decomposers reach only the outside9 pieces · 3 times as much surfacepurple dots =
decomposers
BEFORE · ONE BIG PIECEOnly the outside can be worked onDecomposers work on surfaces. With one big piece, everything in the middle is out of reach until the outside is gone.
AFTER · A DETRITIVORE HAS BEEN AT ITSame leaf, far more surfaceThe amount of leaf has not changed. But cutting it in three each way gives three times as much surface for the same volume: a higher surface-to-volume ratio. Decomposers can now work on all of it at once, so it breaks down much faster.It is the reason you chew your food before your stomach digests it.
10 / 33 · MODULE 2.4 · PART 1 · LOCK IT IN

Lock it in

  1. Energy flows through once. Matter cycles: the same atoms move between organisms and the abiotic environment.
  2. A macronutrient is one needed in large quantities. It is not a large molecule.
  3. When something is eaten, its molecules are taken apart and rebuilt. The atoms are what get passed on. Nitrogen ends up in proteins, DNA and RNA.
  4. Conservation of mass: atoms are never created or destroyed, only rearranged. That is why matter can cycle.
  5. Decomposition turns organic molecules in detritus into inorganic forms producers can use: ammonium, nitrate and phosphate.
  6. Decomposition is faster when it is warm, when moisture is moderate, when there is oxygen, and when the detritus is high quality (soft, not woody).
  7. Detritivores are animals that eat and shred detritus. Smaller pieces have more surface for their volume, so decomposers work faster.

The decomposers: fungi and whale falls

Something has to do the work of decomposition. What kind of living thing is it, and why is most of it hidden?

12 / 33 · PART 2 · 1 OF 8

Who the decomposers are

Part 1 was about what decomposition does. This part is about who does it. One word describes how nearly all of them live, so learn it before you meet them.

INTERACTIVE · TAKE THE WORD APART

CHEMO · WHERE THE ENERGY COMES FROMFrom chemicals, not from lightA chemotroph gets its energy by breaking chemical bonds in molecules. The opposite is photo: energy from sunlight.
HETERO · WHERE THE CARBON COMES FROMFrom other organismsHetero means "other". A heterotroph gets its carbon from organic molecules that some other organism made. The opposite is auto, "self": carbon taken straight from CO₂.
TROPH · FEEDINGIt is a word about how something feeds itselfPut together: a chemoheterotroph gets both its energy and its carbon from organic molecules. One molecule of glucose can supply both. You are one. So is every animal, every fungus, and many bacteria and archaea.
TAP EACH PART OF THE WORDchemo + hetero + trophOne long word, three short ideas. Learn the parts and the word never needs memorizing.
13 / 33 · PART 2 · 2 OF 8

Fungi: the basics

Fungi are one of the major groups of decomposers, and on land they do most of the work. Four things to know about any fungus.

INTERACTIVE · HOW A FUNGUS EATS

AN ANIMALFood goes inside, then gets digestedAn animal takes food into a gut. Digestive enzymes break it down inside the body, and the small molecules are absorbed from there.
A FUNGUSFood is digested outside, then taken inA fungus has no mouth and no gut. It releases digestive enzymes into whatever it is growing through, the enzymes break large molecules into small ones, and the fungus absorbs those. Digestion happens outside the body.Fungi cannot move to find food, so they grow towards it instead.
TAP ONESame kind of feeder, opposite orderBoth are chemoheterotrophs. The pink dots are digestive enzymes. Watch where they are: inside the body, or outside it.
14 / 33 · PART 2 · 3 OF 8

Digest outside, then absorb

A fungus has no mouth and no gut. It feeds by absorbing molecules straight from its surroundings. That way of living creates two problems, and the whole body of a fungus is the answer to them.

INTERACTIVE · ONE HYPHAL TIP IN DEAD WOOD

Release, digest, absorb, grow on

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
HYPHAHYPHAcellulose: too big
to absorbenzymes released
at the tipenzymes cut it
into glucosesmall molecules nowglucose is absorbedtaken in through
the wallthe tip grows onnext food
1 · ENZYMES OUT

The fungus releases digestive enzymes

Big molecules such as cellulose and starch cannot cross into a cell. So the hypha releases enzymes into whatever it is growing through. They are released at the growing tip.

2 · DIGESTION, OUTSIDE THE BODY

The enzymes break the food down

Out in the wood, the enzymes cut cellulose into single glucose molecules. This is extracellular digestion: digestion outside the cell.

3 · ABSORPTION

The small molecules are taken in

Glucose and other small molecules are absorbed straight across the wall and membrane. Feeding by absorbing dissolved molecules is called osmotrophy. A fungus digests first and takes the food in afterward.

4 · ON TO THE NEXT MEAL

It cannot walk, so it grows

A fungus has no way of moving. It finds food by growing. Where food is rich the hyphae grow fast and branch again and again. Where it is poor they slow down or stop.

15 / 33 · PART 2 · 4 OF 8

Chitin: why a fungus has a tough wall

Every fungal cell is wrapped in a wall of chitin. The wall is not there only for protection. It is what lets a thread as thin as a hair force its way through soil and into wood.

INTERACTIVE · ONE HYPHA IN SOIL

Water in, pressure up, tip forward

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
chitin wallwater flows in (osmosis)more dissolved
molecules insidethe chitin wall holds: no burstingTURGORpressure pushes the tip forwardsoil
1 · OSMOSIS

Water flows into the hypha

The inside of a hypha holds more dissolved molecules than the dilute water in soil. So water flows in by osmosis.

2 · THE WALL

Chitin stops it from bursting

A cell with no wall would swell and burst. The chitin wall holds, so the water coming in builds up pressure instead. It is called turgor pressure.

3 · THE PUSH

Pressure drives the tip forward

A hypha grows only at its tip. Turgor pressure provides the force that pushes the tip on, through soil and into wood. That is how a fungus finds its food.

16 / 33 · PART 2 · 5 OF 8

The hidden forest

Ask someone to draw a fungus and they draw a mushroom. That is like drawing an apple and calling it the tree. Most of a fungus, and a surprising share of a whole forest, is underground.

INTERACTIVE · A FOREST, CUT AWAY

What is under the forest floor

Tap a button to explore
ABOVE GROUND · the small part you seeBELOW GROUNDMYCELIUM · all the hyphae togetherone hyphamushroomspuffballbracket fungi on
a living trunkspores
MYCELIUMThe body of the fungus is the networkAll the threads together are the mycelium (plural: mycelia). It runs through the soil, the leaf litter and the wood. This is the fungus. When you walk through a forest you are walking over an enormous amount of it.
ONE HYPHAA single threadOne thread is a hypha (plural: hyphae). Hyphae are 10 to 50 times thinner than a human hair. Being so long and thin gives them a huge surface for absorbing food.A hypha grows only at its tip, and it releases its digestive enzymes there. So growing forward is how a fungus both finds food and digests it.
FRUITING BODIESThe part you actually noticeA mushroom is a fruiting body. So is a white puffball, and so are the shelf-like brackets on a tree trunk. They are built by the mycelium for one job: making and releasing spores.Brackets on a standing tree are a sign that the fungus is already digesting its wood. Fungi do not wait for the tree to fall.
SPORESHow a fungus reproduces and spreadsSpores are tiny cells that rain out of the fruiting body and drift away on the air. One that lands on food can grow into a new mycelium. Spores are produced and dispersed during the fruiting-body stage of the life cycle.
TAP A BUTTON TO LIGHT UP ONE PARTThe mushroom is the tip of the icebergLook at how much of this picture is below the ground line. A mushroom is a small, short-lived part that a far bigger organism pushes up to release spores.

Fungi are one of the most diverse groups of eukaryotes, and they do two big jobs in an ecosystem.

INTERACTIVE · SKETCH MAP · WHERE FUNGAL SPECIES ARE

Not every fungus lives on dead matter. Mycorrhizal fungi grow in and around the roots of living plants. The name means "fungus-root".

19 / 33 · PART 2 · 8 OF 8

Whale falls: one carcass, a whole community

Everything so far has been on land. Decomposition happens in water too, with one main difference in what sets the speed.

INTERACTIVE · WHAT HAPPENS TO A DEAD WHALE

A whale fall, stage by stage

Tap the buttons, or Next stage, to click through all 4
sunlit surface · where the whale feddeep sea · cold, dark, little fooda whale dies
and sinksSTAGE 1 · the fleshhagfishsharkcrabsSTAGE 2 · the bonesSNOTWORMS
growing on the bonesBACTERIA
purple matsAFTERWARDS · open questionswhere do the young
snotworms go next?
THE FALLA whale dies near the surface and sinksThe whale spent its life feeding in the sunlit upper ocean. When it dies, all of that organic matter sinks to the sea floor, where food is scarce. The carcass links two biomes: matter made near the surface now feeds the deep.
STAGE 1 · SCAVENGERSFlesh-eating animals arrive firstOnce the carcass is on the bottom, mobile scavengers find it and eat the soft tissue: hagfish, sharks, crabs and other arthropods. They strip the flesh down to the skeleton.
STAGE 2 · THE SKELETONThen the bones are eaten tooWith the flesh gone, a different community takes over. Bacteria feed on what is left in and around the bones. Snotworms, bone-eating worms, grow on the skeleton itself.It is cold down here, and temperature is a key driver of decomposition in water, so this stage is slow.
AFTERWARDSA lot is still unknownA whale fall is a rare island of food in a huge, empty sea floor. Snotworms need bones to live on. So when one skeleton is used up, where do they go, and how do their young find the next one? Nobody is sure yet. Much about these communities is still being worked out.
20 / 33 · MODULE 2.4 · PART 2 · LOCK IT IN

Lock it in

  1. A chemoheterotroph gets its energy and its carbon from organic molecules. Decomposers are chemoheterotrophs that feed on detritus.
  2. Decomposers are bacteria, archaea and fungi, plus a few other eukaryotes: all three domains.
  3. Fungi are eukaryotes, closely related to animals. They release enzymes, digest outside the body (extracellular digestion), and absorb the small molecules (osmotrophy).
  4. Their cell walls are chitin. Water flows in by osmosis, the wall holds, and the turgor pressure pushes the hyphal tip forward.
  5. Most fungi are multicellular: thin hyphae, with a huge surface for their volume, form a mycelium. The mushroom is only the fruiting body, which releases spores. Yeasts are the single-celled fungi.
  6. Much of a forest's biomass is underground, and about 50% of that is fungal tissue.
  7. There are an estimated 0.8 to 5.1 million fungal species. Diversity is greatest at the equator, and precipitation is the strongest predictor.
  8. Mycorrhizal fungi help plants take up phosphate and get sugars in return. It is a trade: it costs the plant 4% to 20% of its carbohydrate.
  9. In water, temperature is a key driver. A whale fall carries matter from the surface to the deep sea: scavengers first, then snotworms and bacteria on the bones.

The nitrogen cycle

Now put the pools and the fluxes together. Nitrogen starts in the air as N₂ gas, gets pulled into living things by microbes, moves through the food web, and is returned by microbes.

Every form of nitrogen is a stop on the map. Every step is a numbered arrow, and the list under the map uses the same numbers and colors. The drawings further down take the steps one at a time, in these same colors.

Denitrification: usable nitrogen goes back to the air

Fixation is the door in. Denitrification is the door out. Where there is no oxygen, microbes turn nitrate back into N₂ gas, and that nitrogen is out of reach again.

INTERACTIVE · SAME SOIL, TWO CONDITIONS

WITH OXYGEN

Nothing is lost

The spaces between soil grains hold air. Microbes respire with oxygen, as most organisms do. Nitrate stays in the soil, and roots take it up.

NO OXYGEN

Nitrate is used in place of oxygen

Water has filled the spaces, and the oxygen is used up. Denitrifying microbes switch to nitrate for their respiration. The nitrogen comes out as N₂ gas and bubbles away. The soil now holds less usable nitrogen.

The phosphorus cycle

Phosphorus moves through pools just as nitrogen does, but it starts somewhere very different, and part of its journey is extremely slow.

EVERY STEP · THE WHOLE PHOSPHORUS CYCLE ON ONE CARD

Rock to rock: eight arrows, one usable form, and no gas

Phosphorus is simpler than nitrogen. Most of it is in rock, not in the air. Producers use one form, the phosphate ion, PO₄³⁻. No microbe has to change it into another form first.

ROCKPO₄³⁻ in soilSEASEDIMENT12345678
1Weathering
phosphate locked in rock→PO₄³⁻ in soil and water
PHOSPHORUS ENTERS THE FOOD WEBWho: no organism. Rock breaks down chemically.Speed: slow.
2Uptake and assimilation
PO₄³⁻ in soil, or in the water column→ATP, nucleic acids, phospholipids
INORGANIC → ORGANICWho: primary producers. On land, mycorrhizal fungi help. In water, it comes from the water column.Speed: fast.
3Feeding
producer's molecules→consumer's molecules
Who: consumers. Their P atoms come from food.Speed: fast.
4Decomposition
detritus→PO₄³⁻
ORGANIC → INORGANICWho: decomposers. Some phosphate is taken straight back up. Some is carried away by water.Speed: fast.
5Runoff
PO₄³⁻ in soil→rivers, lakes, the sea
Who: no organism. Water carries it. Fertilizer washed off fields adds more and drives eutrophication.Speed: slow.
6The same fast loop, in the water
PO₄³⁻ in the water column→producers→consumers→decomposers
Who: phytoplankton, their consumers, and decomposers, in sunlit water. Upwelling can bring phosphate back up from deep water.Speed: fast.
7Sedimentation
phosphorus in the sea→sediment on the sea floor
PHOSPHORUS LEAVES THE FOOD WEBWho: no organism. What sinks builds up on the sea floor.Speed: very slow.
8Tectonic uplift
sediment→rock in mountains
Who: no organism. Sediments are raised into mountains, and weathering can start again.Speed: the slowest step of all.
FAST INSIDE, SLOW OUTSIDE Arrows 2, 3, 4 and 6 are the fast loops: phosphate moves quickly through plants and animals. Arrows 1, 5, 7 and 8 move phosphorus through soil, ocean and rock, and they are very slow. That is what slows the whole cycle.
THREE WAYS IT DIFFERS FROM NITROGEN The big pool is rock, not the atmosphere. There is one usable form, not two. And no step needs a microbe to change the form: phosphate is only passed along, taken up, eaten and released.

Dead zones

Humans now fix about as much nitrogen as nature does, and most of it goes onto fields. What is not taken up by crops runs off. Follow it downstream.

INTERACTIVE · SIX STEPS FROM FERTILIZER TO DEAD ZONE

Step through the chain of events

Tap Next step to go through all 6
FARMLANDO₂SEA FLOORNPNnutrients wash inALGAL BLOOMalgae die and sinkHUGE DETRITAL POOLdecomposers multiplyDEAD ZONEalmost no oxygen
1 OF 6 · NUTRIENTS ARRIVEInorganic nitrogen and phosphorus wash inRain carries excess fertilizer off farmland into streams and rivers. The Mississippi River delivers it to the Gulf of Mexico.
2 OF 6 · A BLOOMPhytoplankton grow explosivelyHere, nitrogen and phosphorus were the limiting nutrients: the ones in short supply. With the limit lifted, algae multiply into a "harmful" bloom. So far this is just eutrophication.
3 OF 6 · THE BLOOM DIESPhytoplankton diePhytoplankton are short-lived. A huge bloom means a huge number of dead cells, and they sink.
4 OF 6 · DEAD MATTER PILES UPA huge detrital poolAll that dead algae is detritus: a mountain of organic matter on the bottom, far more than usual.
5 OF 6 · DECOMPOSERS BOOMDecomposers increaseMore food for decomposers means more decomposers. Their population grows to match the detritus.
6 OF 6 · OXYGEN RUNS OUTOxygen declines: a dead zoneDecomposers carry out cellular respiration, which uses oxygen. So many of them use it faster than it is replaced. Oxygen in the water falls so low that fish and other animals leave or die.The process that removes the oxygen is cellular respiration by decomposers. Not the nutrients, and not the algae while they are alive.
32 / 33 · MODULE 2.4 · PART 3 · LOCK IT IN

Lock it in

  1. Nitrogen builds proteins and nucleic acids. Phosphorus builds ATP, nucleic acids and phospholipids.
  2. Producers take up ammonium, nitrate and phosphate and assimilate them. Heterotrophs get N and P from food.
  3. A pool (reservoir) is where an element is. A flux is the element moving. Detritus is a pool.
  4. The largest nitrogen pool is the atmosphere, and most producers cannot use it directly.
  5. Nitrogen fixation (N₂ → ammonia) is done only by some bacteria and archaea, such as Rhizobium in legume nodules. Denitrification sends nitrogen back to the air.
  6. Decomposition returns nitrogen and phosphorus from detritus to inorganic forms.
  7. Phosphate cycles quickly through organisms but very slowly through soil and ocean.
  8. Extra nutrients → bloom → algae die → detritus → decomposers → oxygen declines: a dead zone.

Quiz

62 questions on matter cycles, decomposition, fungi, whale falls, and the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles. Pick an answer to see whether it is right and why.

QUESTION 1 OF 62What does it mean to say that energy flows but matter cycles?

Correct. Not quite. Energy is a one-way flow. Atoms move between organisms and the abiotic environment in a loop.

QUESTION 2 OF 62A macronutrient is a nutrient that is:

Correct. Not quite. Macro refers to how much is needed. The word for a big molecule is macromolecule.

QUESTION 3 OF 62A limiting nutrient is one that:

Correct. Not quite. Nitrogen and phosphorus are limiting in some ecosystems, not in all of them.

QUESTION 4 OF 62A giraffe eats a leaf that contains protein. What ends up in the giraffe?

Correct. Not quite. Digestion breaks the protein into amino acids. The giraffe builds its own proteins from them. Atoms are passed on, molecules are not.

QUESTION 5 OF 62Which of these molecules does NOT contain nitrogen?

Correct. Not quite. Carbohydrates are carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. Proteins and nucleic acids contain nitrogen.

QUESTION 6 OF 62The law of conservation of mass means that during decomposition:

Correct. Not quite. That is why an atom that was once in a dinosaur can be in you: the atom was never used up.

QUESTION 7 OF 62Decomposition starts with ___ molecules and ends with ___ molecules.

Correct. Not quite. Decomposers break complex organic molecules in detritus down into inorganic forms producers can take up.

QUESTION 8 OF 62Which set lists inorganic forms that producers can take up?

Correct. Not quite. NH₄⁺ and NO₃⁻ supply nitrogen, and phosphate supplies phosphorus.

QUESTION 9 OF 62What do decomposers do with the energy in detritus?

Correct. Not quite. Decomposers recycle atoms, not energy.

QUESTION 10 OF 62On the graph of decomposer activity against soil water content, each line rises and then falls. Why does activity fall in very wet soil?

Correct. Not quite. Water fills the gaps between soil grains and pushes the air out. Most decomposers need oxygen.

QUESTION 11 OF 62The same graph has separate lines for 10, 20 and 30 °C. What do the three lines together show?

Correct. Not quite. The 30 °C line sits above the 20 °C line, which sits above the 10 °C line.

QUESTION 12 OF 62In waterlogged, oxygen-poor places such as bogs, dead plant matter tends to:

Correct. Not quite. Fungi need oxygen to break down woody tissue. Buried, undecayed plant matter is what eventually becomes coal.

QUESTION 13 OF 62"High-quality" detritus is detritus that:

Correct. Not quite. In ecology, high quality means easy and rewarding for decomposers. It breaks down fast.

QUESTION 14 OF 62Why does wood decompose so much more slowly than a green leaf?

Correct. Not quite. Lignin has no regular structure for an enzyme to grip. Fungi do most of the decomposition of wood.

QUESTION 15 OF 62An earthworm eating dead leaves is best described as a:

Correct. Not quite. Detritivores are animals that eat detritus and break it into smaller pieces.

QUESTION 16 OF 62How do detritivores speed up decomposition?

Correct. Not quite. Same volume, more surface. It is the reason you chew food before digesting it.

QUESTION 17 OF 62Which list names the major groups of decomposers?

Correct. Not quite. All three domains are represented: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya (the fungi, plus a few other eukaryotes).

QUESTION 18 OF 62A chemoheterotroph gets its energy from ___ and its carbon from ___.

Correct. Not quite. Chemo: energy from chemicals. Hetero: carbon from molecules made by other organisms. Animals and fungi are both chemoheterotrophs.

QUESTION 19 OF 62Which domain includes the fungi?

Correct. Not quite. Fungi are eukaryotes, and their closest relatives are animals, not plants.

QUESTION 20 OF 62How does a fungus feed?

Correct. Not quite. Digestion is external. Animals eat first and digest inside. Fungi digest first and absorb.

QUESTION 21 OF 62Fungal cell walls are made of:

Correct. Not quite. Chitin is the same material as the exoskeleton of arthropods.

QUESTION 22 OF 62Which statement about fungi is correct?

Correct. Not quite. Most fungi are built of threads called hyphae. Yeasts grow as single cells.

QUESTION 23 OF 62One thread of a fungus is a ___, and the whole network of threads is the ___.

Correct. Not quite. Hypha (plural hyphae) is one thread. Mycelium (plural mycelia) is all of them together.

QUESTION 24 OF 62A mushroom is:

Correct. Not quite. Most of the fungus is the mycelium, hidden in soil and wood. Puffballs are fruiting bodies too.

QUESTION 25 OF 62Much of the biomass of a forest is underground. About how much of that underground biomass is fungal tissue?

Correct. Not quite. Fungi are common in forests, not rare. Their mycelia are roughly half of what lives below ground.

QUESTION 26 OF 62What is the strongest predictor of how many fungal species an area has?

Correct. Not quite. Diversity is greatest at the equator and declines toward the poles, but rainfall predicts it best. Soil properties such as pH matter too.

QUESTION 27 OF 62How does fungal diversity change from the equator toward the poles, compared with plant diversity?

Correct. Not quite. There are still many fungal species in cool northern forests.

QUESTION 28 OF 62What do mycorrhizal fungi and their plants exchange?

Correct. Not quite. It is a mutualism. About 85% of land plant species have these associations.

QUESTION 29 OF 62In aquatic environments, a key driver of decomposition rates is:

Correct. Not quite. Cold, deep water slows decomposition.

QUESTION 30 OF 62What happens first when a whale carcass reaches the sea floor?

Correct. Not quite. Flesh-eating scavengers arrive first. Bone-eating snotworms and bacteria work on the skeleton afterwards.

QUESTION 31 OF 62Whale populations were once 6 to 20 times higher than they are now. What does that mean for the deep sea?

Correct. Not quite. Carcasses link the surface ocean to the sea floor, so fewer whales at the surface is felt at the bottom.

QUESTION 32 OF 62Which molecules contain phosphorus?

Correct. Not quite. Phospholipids, which build every cell membrane, are the main use of phosphorus in a cell.

QUESTION 33 OF 62How do nitrogen and phosphorus move up a food chain?

Correct. Not quite. Eating a producer is herbivory, and eating an animal is predation. Either way the atoms move up inside organic molecules.

QUESTION 34 OF 62Which of these is a pool, not a flux?

Correct. Not quite. A pool is where the element is. Detritus is a place nitrogen sits. The other three are movements.

QUESTION 35 OF 62Which is the largest pool of nitrogen?

Correct. Not quite. The atmosphere holds it as N₂ gas, which most producers cannot use directly.

QUESTION 36 OF 62Why can most organisms not use N₂ gas?

Correct. Not quite. Only some bacteria and archaea have the enzyme to break it.

QUESTION 37 OF 62Nitrogen fixation is:

Correct. Not quite. Fixation and assimilation are different steps. Fixation makes nitrogen usable. Assimilation builds it into organic molecules.

QUESTION 38 OF 62Which domains contain organisms that can fix nitrogen?

Correct. Not quite. No plant, animal or fungus can do it by itself.

QUESTION 39 OF 62Rhizobium are ___ that live in ___ and carry out ___.

Correct. Not quite. They take N₂ from the atmospheric reservoir and produce NH₄⁺. They are not the only nitrogen fixers.

QUESTION 40 OF 62What are the two natural kinds of nitrogen fixation, and which is more common?

Correct. Not quite. Lightning breaks the triple bond with raw energy, but it is a small share of the total.

QUESTION 41 OF 62Which forms of nitrogen can primary producers take up?

Correct. Not quite. Roots take them from the soil. Phytoplankton take them straight from the water.

QUESTION 42 OF 62Nitrification is the conversion of:

Correct. Not quite. Nitrifying bacteria and archaea swap the hydrogens for oxygens, NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻. They use O₂, and they get energy from doing it.

QUESTION 43 OF 62Denitrification:

Correct. Not quite. It is the reverse of fixation, and it removes usable nitrogen from soil or water.

QUESTION 44 OF 62What is the shortest path for a nitrogen atom from an elephant seal to a baleen whale?

Correct. Not quite. No feeding path leads from a seal to a baleen whale, so the atom must go down through decomposers and back up through producers.

QUESTION 45 OF 62How is the phosphorus cycle different from the nitrogen cycle?

Correct. Not quite. Phosphate moves quickly through organisms but very slowly through soil and ocean.

QUESTION 46 OF 62Hippos graze on land at night and rest in rivers by day. In nutrient-cycle terms, they:

Correct. Not quite. That movement is a flux between two pools, carried inside an animal.

QUESTION 47 OF 62In the dry season, what is the effect of MANY hippos on a river pool?

Correct. Not quite. A few hippos fertilize the river and raise NPP. Too many overload it.

QUESTION 48 OF 62Put the dead-zone chain in order.

Correct. Not quite. Six links. Know them in order.

QUESTION 49 OF 62What directly causes the oxygen in a dead zone to fall?

Correct. Not quite. Not the nutrients, and not the algae while they are alive.

QUESTION 50 OF 62Hypoxia means ___ and anoxia means ___.

Correct. Not quite. Hypo means under, an means without. Hypoxia is usually defined as less than 2 mg of oxygen per liter.

QUESTION 51 OF 62Where do most of the excess nitrogen and phosphorus reaching the Gulf of Mexico come from?

Correct. Not quite. Crops and pasture together supply about 71% of the nitrogen and 80% of the phosphorus.

QUESTION 52 OF 62Osmotrophy means:

Correct. Not quite. A fungus digests outside its body first (extracellular digestion), then absorbs the small dissolved molecules. That absorbing is osmotrophy.

QUESTION 53 OF 62Water flows into a hypha by osmosis. Why does the hypha not burst?

Correct. Not quite. The wall turns incoming water into pressure. That turgor pressure is the force that drives the growing tip through soil and wood.

QUESTION 54 OF 62Which kind of mycorrhiza branches inside root cells as arbuscules and matters most for phosphorus?

Correct. Not quite. Endo means inside. Ectomycorrhizae form a sheath around the root tip and help with nitrogen.

QUESTION 55 OF 62A plant pays its mycorrhizal fungus 4% to 20% of its carbohydrate. In a heavily fertilized field, what happens?

Correct. Not quite. It is a trade, not a gift. When the soil already supplies plenty of nutrients, the plant does not pay for help it does not need.

QUESTION 56 OF 62In 231 potato field trials, what did adding a mycorrhizal fungus do?

Correct. Not quite. 38.3 tons per hectare without added fungus, 42.2 with it (Hijri 2016). Field soil already had some fungus, so this is extra fungus against none added.

QUESTION 57 OF 62Where does denitrification happen?

Correct. Not quite. Denitrifiers use nitrate in place of oxygen. Where there is oxygen, they use oxygen and the nitrate stays in the soil.

QUESTION 58 OF 62Why do denitrifying microbes turn nitrate into N₂?

Correct. Not quite. This is anaerobic respiration. The microbe is getting energy, not trying to remove nitrogen.

QUESTION 59 OF 62During nitrification, ammonium passes through which halfway form?

Correct. Not quite. NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻. Nitrifying bacteria and archaea do it with oxygen, as their energy source.

QUESTION 60 OF 62Anammox:

Correct. Not quite. Short for anaerobic ammonia oxidation. Like denitrification, it sends nitrogen back to the air.

QUESTION 61 OF 62Which step of the phosphorus cycle is the slowest of all?

Correct. Not quite. Uptake, feeding and decomposition are the fast loops. Weathering, runoff, sedimentation and uplift are slow, and uplift is slowest.

QUESTION 62 OF 62Which statement about the phosphorus cycle is correct?

Correct. Not quite. Most phosphorus is in rock. There is no gas, and phosphate is only passed along, taken up, eaten and released.

Guiding questions · Matter and decomposition

These are the questions this module is built to answer. Try each one from memory, then tap it to check.

Q1  What does it mean to say that energy flows but matter cycles? What is the “matter” to which we are referring? Where is it cycling?

Energy flows: it enters as sunlight, passes through a food web once, and leaves as heat.

Matter cycles: the matter is atoms, such as carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus. The same atoms are used again and again.

They cycle between organisms and the abiotic environment: soil, water and air.

Q2  If a giraffe (or other organism) eats a leaf that contains protein, does the unchanged protein molecule pass into the giraffe? Is it the same protein in the giraffe as in the leaf?

No. Digestion breaks the leaf's protein into amino acids. The giraffe builds its own proteins from them (biosynthesis).

The nitrogen atoms are the same. The protein is not.

Q3  How do temperature and moisture influence decomposition in terrestrial environments? How does detritus quality influence decomposition? What factors influence decomposition in aquatic environments?

Temperature: warmer is faster, across the range measured.

Moisture: moderate is fastest. Too dry and decomposers cannot work. Too wet and the soil runs short of oxygen.

Detritus quality: high-quality detritus (rich in nitrogen, low in lignin) decomposes quickly. Low-quality detritus (woody, high in lignin) decomposes slowly.

In water: temperature is a key driver.

Q4  What types of organisms are decomposers? What do they do in an ecosystem? Does decomposition start with organic or inorganic molecules? Does it result in organic or inorganic molecules?

Bacteria, archaea and fungi, plus a few other eukaryotes.

They cycle nutrients from the detrital pool back to the abiotic environment.

Decomposition starts with organic molecules and results in inorganic forms, such as ammonium, nitrate and phosphate, which producers can use.

Q5  What types of organisms are detritivores? What do they do in an ecosystem?

Animals that eat detritus: earthworms, termites, dung beetles, millipedes, and many crabs and lobsters.

They break detritus into smaller pieces. Smaller pieces have more surface for their volume, so decomposers can work faster.

Guiding questions · Fungi and whale falls

These are the questions this module is built to answer. Try each one from memory, then tap it to check.

Q6  What Domain are fungi in: Archaea, Bacteria, or Eukarya? What does it mean to say that fungi are chemoheterotrophs? Where do fungi digest their food? What are cell walls of fungi made of?

Eukarya.

Chemoheterotroph: they get both their energy and their carbon from organic molecules.

They digest food outside the body: they release digestive enzymes and then absorb the nutrients. Digesting outside is extracellular digestion, and absorbing the dissolved molecules is osmotrophy.

Cell walls are made of chitin, a complex carbohydrate, the same material as arthropod exoskeletons. The wall holds as water flows in, so turgor pressure pushes the hyphal tip forward.

Q7  Are fungi common in forests or rare? Are there many species of fungi or few? How does fungal diversity change with latitude? What factors influence fungal species richness?

Common. Much of a forest's biomass is underground, and about 50% of that is fungal tissue.

Many: an estimated 0.8 to 5.1 million species.

Diversity is greatest at the equator and declines toward the poles, less sharply than plant diversity does.

The strongest predictor is mean annual precipitation. Soil properties such as pH also matter.

Q8  Are fungi unicellular or multicellular? What are hyphae? What are mycelia? What is an example of a fruiting body? In which part of fungal life cycle are spores produced and dispersed?

Both exist. Most are multicellular. Yeasts are unicellular.

Hyphae are the thin threads that make up the body. Mycelia are whole networks of hyphae.

A mushroom is a fruiting body. So is a puffball.

Spores are produced and dispersed at the fruiting-body stage.

Q9  What do mycorrhizal fungi help plants take up? How common are associations between mycorrhizal fungi and land plants?

Phosphate. In return the plant gives the fungus carbohydrates: 4% to 20% of all it makes.

Endomycorrhizae grow into root cells and matter most for phosphorus. Ectomycorrhizae sheath the root tip and help with nitrogen.

Very common: about 85% of land plant species, also given as more than 90% of land plants.

Q10  What are whale falls? What are some examples of species that live in these communities?

A whale fall is a dead whale that has sunk to the sea floor, and the community that lives on it.

Scavengers (fish such as hagfish and sharks, and crabs) eat the flesh. Snotworms, bone-eating worms, live on the skeleton. Bacteria feed on the bones and the mud around them.

Guiding questions · Nitrogen and phosphorus

These are the questions this module is built to answer. Try each one from memory, then tap it to check.

Q11  What are some examples of molecules that have phosphorus in them? What are some examples of molecules that have nitrogen in them? How do nitrogen and phosphorus move through the food chain? Who recycles them? What does it mean to say they are “recycled”?

Phosphorus: ATP, nucleic acids, phospholipids. Nitrogen: proteins and nucleic acids.

They move up the food chain by consumption: each consumer digests its food and rebuilds the atoms into its own molecules.

Decomposers recycle them. Recycled means the same atoms are released from dead matter in inorganic form and taken up by producers again.

Q12  What is a “pool” of a nutrient? What are two other terms that mean the same thing as “pool” in this context? What is a “flux” of a nutrient?

A pool is a place where the nutrient is held: the atmosphere, soil, water, organisms, detritus.

Reservoir and compartment mean the same thing.

A flux is the movement of the nutrient from one pool to another.

Q13  What is the largest pool of nitrogen? Is the nitrogen in the largest pool directly accessible to most primary producers? What are some important fluxes of nitrogen? What is nitrogen fixation? What domain(s) contains organisms that carry out nitrogen fixation: Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya? What is denitrification?

The atmosphere, as N₂ gas. No, most producers cannot use it directly.

Fluxes: nitrogen fixation, nitrification, uptake and assimilation, feeding, decomposition, denitrification.

Nitrogen fixation turns N₂ gas into ammonia. It is done by some Bacteria and Archaea only.

Denitrification turns nitrate back into N₂ gas, only where there is no oxygen, as in waterlogged soil. The microbes respire with nitrate in place of oxygen.

Q14  What forms of nitrogen are accessible to (meaning: can be taken up by) primary producers?

Ammonium (NH₄⁺) and nitrate (NO₃⁻).

Q15  In what domain are Rhizobium? Why are they important in the nitrogen cycle? Are they the only organisms that can carry out this process? In what type of plants do Rhizobium live?

Bacteria. They fix nitrogen: they take N₂ from the atmosphere and produce NH₄⁺ that the plant can use.

No. Free-living bacteria and archaea in soil, and Trichodesmium in the ocean, fix nitrogen too.

They live in nodules on the roots of legumes.

Q16  What are the two “natural” types of nitrogen fixation? Which is more common? What are the human sources of fixed nitrogen? Do these go in different places on the small-scale nitrogen cycle diagram?

Biological fixation and lightning. Biological fixation is far more common.

Human sources: nitrogen fertilizer made industrially, nitrogen-fixing crops, and fossil fuels.

No. They all enter at the same place: the nitrogen fixation arrow, turning N₂ into usable nitrogen.

Q17  How do hippos move nutrients between land and water? Roughly what percent of the nitrogen and phosphorus in the Mara River in Kenya comes from hippos? What effect do hippos have on net primary productivity in the Mara River in the dry season if there are few hippos? What if there are a lot of hippos in the dry season? What effects do hippos have on grasslands?

They graze on land at night and release dung and urine into the river by day, carrying nitrogen and phosphorus from land to water. Hippos supply a large share of the river's nitrogen and phosphorus: one estimate is that they raise it by about 25% (Subalusky and colleagues, 2015).

Few hippos, dry season: the nutrients act as fertilizer, and NPP goes up.

Many hippos, dry season: too much dung. Decomposers use up the oxygen, fish die, and NPP goes down.

On grassland: grazing makes the grass stubbier and leafier, which is more nutritious.

Q18  What is the sequence of events that starts with excess fertilizer and ends with a dead zone in the Gulf of Mexico? What process causes the concentration of oxygen dissolved in the water to decrease?

Nutrients wash in → phytoplankton bloom → phytoplankton die → a huge detrital pool → decomposers increase → oxygen declines.

The oxygen falls because of cellular respiration by decomposers.

Q19  Where do the excess nitrogen and phosphorus that reach the Gulf of Mexico come from?

Mostly from farming in the land drained by the Mississippi River: fertilizer on crops such as corn and soybeans, and pasture. Urban sources and deposition from the air add smaller shares.
